POLICY: GEOPOLITICAL TETRIS. Illustration by Sarah Durrani Tetris is an interestingly simple but challenging game. Blocks of different shapes descend on to a confined board and the player must continuously find space to accommodate them. Every placement affects the next move. As the board fills, choices diminish, mistakes become increasingly expensive, and even the right piece arriving at the wrong time can become a problem. The evolving global geopolitical landscape bears an astonishing resemblance to this game. Yet the intrinsic simplicity of the game is missing: the blocks are getting larger, time and space are shrinking, and states have less freedom to position themselves without new vulnerabilities. A bird’s eye view of the prevailing environment reveals that Russia remains locked in Ukraine in a contest it portrays in terms of security, strategic identity and its place in the European order. Europe, meanwhile, is grappling with the perceived long-term threat from Russia, the burden of sustaining Ukraine, changing ties with Washington, the demands for greater burden-sharing, energy insecurity and sluggish growth. Long-standing assumptions underpinning European security no longer appear immutable. In the Middle East, the widening confrontation involving Iran, Israel and the United States has transformed an already unstable region, where escalation can have consequences far beyond its geographical boundaries. A prolonged crisis in the Gulf can rapidly translate into higher energy costs, inflation, disrupted supply chains and slower growth in South and Southeast Asia. As global power shifts, the world gets reconfigured and crises become increasingly interconnected, Pakistan must decide which relationships to prioritise — and which commitments it can no longer afford Amid this deafening strategic noise, China has displayed what may be described as strategic restraint. Beijing has enormous economic stakes in the stability of the Middle East and the international trading system, yet it prefers to remain cautious of direct entanglement in these conflicts. Whether this represents deliberate patience or a preference to let others exhaust themselves is debatable. China’s willingness to help shape the emerging order remains uncertain. Such is perhaps the defining characteristic of today’s geopolitical Tetris: the pieces are no longer independent of one another. A conflict in Ukraine alters Europe’s security and energy calculations. War in the Middle East affects Asian economies. Competition between Washington and Beijing influences technology, trade, investment and supply chains across continents. Global interdependence has erased the geographical separation between crises. The question, therefore, is not how individual crises will end, but what international system will emerge as the pieces settle. THREE WAYS TO READ THE BOARD Let us see how various schools of thought view the changing global landscape. Offensive realism holds that great powers operating in an uncertain international system seek power, favourable balances and regional predominance, because they cannot entrust their survival to the intentions of others. Viewed through this prism, the present turbulence may represent less an aberration than a redistribution of global power. Such an order may contain several poles yet revolve predominantly around two centres of gravity: the US and China. Russia, India, Europe and other consequential powers will occupy important spaces, but much of international politics could increasingly be influenced by competition between Washington and Beijing. At its extreme, this could produce informal spheres of influence, accompanied by expectations of non-interference in each other’s core strategic spaces. Another view sees the turbulence of [US President Donald] Trump 2.0 as a disruption rather than the definitive end of the US-led international order. Institutions, alliances, financial networks and economic relationships built over eight decades possess considerable resilience. A post-Trump US could return to its traditional alliances and restore much of the tone and tenor of the previous order, albeit under changed circumstances. A third viewpoint holds that the emerging system may be neither conventionally bipolar nor genuinely multipolar. It could become an untidy combination of both, with several centres of power operating beneath an overarching US-China rivalry. A country may depend upon China for infrastructure, the US for technology and finance, the Gulf for energy, Europe for exports and another state for security cooperation. Geopolitical blocs increasingly overlap. This is almost the projection of the existing fragmented order in a more orderly manner. WHERE PAKISTAN FITS For Pakistan, this geopolitical Tetris raises several practical questions. Should Pakistan lean towards China or rebalance towards the US? Should it privilege its Gulf relationships or accommodate Iran? Should regional connectivity or traditional security considerations determine its approach towards India? In my view, Pakistan must equally avoid strategic overextension. It neither has the economic capacity nor needs the ambition to seek a leading role in global geopolitics. Its priorities should remain economic growth, development, political stability and regional integration. Strategic relevance should follow national strength, rather than become a substitute for it. There is, however, a limit to how long strategic optionality can be preserved. As in Tetris, the available space diminishes with every falling block. The time may be approaching when Pakistan will have to make harder choices, use the lifelines available to it and place some blocks decisively before the space to manoeuvre disappears altogether. Strategic autonomy should therefore not become an excuse for indecision. Pakistan must have the confidence to say no when its vital interests are compromised, say yes when enduring national interests converge, and exercise restraint when involvement would overstretch its capabilities without commensurate gains. The test should not be who is asking, but what serves Pakistan’s long term national interests. If the world evolves towards a sharper US China bipolarity, Pakistan should avoid becoming a frontline state in their competition. But it cannot disregard the depth, geography and strategic significance of its relationship with China. China should remain Pakistan’s principal strategic anchor, while Islamabad preserves the scope for productive relations with the US, wherever interests converge. If a multipolar order emerges, Pakistan should exploit the greater diplomatic space it offers. Stronger economic and political engagement with the US, Russia, Europe, the Gulf, Iran, Türkiye and Central Asia can coexist with its relationship with China. But multipolarity offers greater room for manoeuvre only to a Pakistan economically strong to use it. However, if the US-led order regains much of its earlier character after the Trump era, Pakistan should avoid both unnecessary confrontation with it and a return to dependency that characterised earlier phases of the relationship. Engagement with Washington should remain substantive and mutually beneficial, without being at the expense of relationships that serve Pakistan’s longer-term interests. THE DOMESTIC FOUNDATION One constant across all three eventualities is that Pakistan’s future lies principally in its own region. China will remain its neighbour and strategic partner; Central Asia will remain a potential gateway for connectivity; Iran and Afghanistan will continue to influence its western security environment; the Gulf will remain vital for energy, investment and economic linkages; and India will remain a neighbour with which competition must be managed and a more stable modus vivendi sought. However, no external relationship, however strong, can compensate for domestic weakness. A weak economy constrains foreign policy choices before external demands even arise. Our strategic investment must therefore remain domestic, focusing on economic growth, political stability, human development, energy security, stronger institutions, technological capacity and the expansion of our productive base. Pakistan does not need to be present at every geopolitical table, mediate every conflict or seek relevance in every contest. There is strategic wisdom in knowing where not to become involved. A state overstretched abroad while economically fragile at home eventually discovers that visibility is not the same as influence. The emerging world order may be bipolar, multipolar or a modified restoration of the old order. Pakistan cannot determine which will take shape, but it can determine whether it enters that order economically vulnerable and strategically dependent, or internally stronger, regionally integrated and confident enough to make choices on its own terms. Tetris offers one final lesson: a player cannot wait indefinitely for the perfect block. Decisions must be made with the pieces available and the space that remains. For Pakistan, that moment may be approaching. The challenge is to recognise which options are worth preserving and which choices can no longer be postponed. Pakistan cannot determine the shape or sequence of the blocks descending on to the geopolitical board. But it can strengthen its foundations, secure its regional space and choose its placements wisely. In the emerging geopolitical Tetris, survival may depend not on fitting everywhere, but on knowing where Pakistan truly belongs. The writer is a retired lieutenant general of the Pakistan Army and president of the Islamabad Policy Research Institute Published in Dawn, EOS, November 1st, 2026

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs352.59 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs382.25 on Nov 6 (Friday), according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra). The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. Under an arrangement announced on Monday for 30 days, oil refineries will contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This allows a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price at the consumer end. Addressing a press conference on Tuesday, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik said efforts were being made to introduce a similar system for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG). Meanwhile, the Jamaat-i-Islami and the government are set to follow up on their recent discussions on possible relief in petroleum prices and hold another round of talks on Thursday, the party said. Rise in fuel prices The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50pc for three months. On Sept 13, PM Shehbaz also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, the petroleum minister announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Pakistan builds record reserves amid Gulf war. KARACHI: Despite the Gulf war’s impact on weaker economies and uncertainty over high oil prices, Pakistan’s foreign exchange reserves climbed to a record high of more than $26.8 billion, the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) reported on Thursday. The war started on Feb 28, jolting many economies, including Pakistan, but the SBP has since improved its reserves and added over $5bn. The SBP’s reserves were $16.568bn in February, rising to $21.568bn on Oct 30. The central bank reported that the foreign exchange holdings of the SBP and commercial banks increased during the week. During the week, SBP reserves rose by $39m. The financial sector considers the State Bank’s current reserves sufficient to keep the exchange rate stable and to encourage exporters to repatriate export proceeds without delay. A stable exchange rate also provides confidence to importers. However, currency experts believe the rupee is overvalued, allowing importers to get cheaper dollars, which is why the trade deficit is widening each month. The trade deficit during July-Oct FY27 reached $14.6bn. The imports were $26bn and exports $11.4bn. It is also believed that the exchange rate is being kept stable at the expense of remittances, which have been increasing each year. The government or the State Bank has not devised a policy to use remittances better; instead, they are used to fill the trade gap. SBP data showed that commercial bank reserves also increased by $70m during the week, reflecting that outflows from Pakistan were less than inflows into the banks. The State Bank reported that the total reserves of the country reached a record high of $26.864bn, compared to $26.754bn last week, an increase of $110m. Published in Dawn, November 6th, 2026

First Marble City being set up in Karachi. KARACHI: Sindh Minister for Information, Transport and Mass Transit Sharjeel Inam Memon has said that Pakistan’s first Marble City is being established in Karachi to create new investment opportunities, promote industrial activities and generate employment. He said the project would enable the processing of marble and granite reserves found in different parts of Sindh and other areas of the country through modern industrial techniques to produce high-quality products for export to international markets. Addressing the pre-launch ceremony of the Karachi Marble City Industrial Park at a local hotel, he said investors would be provided with opportunities to establish industries equipped with modern facilities. The project would promote the local processing of natural resources and the production of finished goods instead of exporting them as raw materials, which would also benefit the national economy, he added. Sindh minister says project will promote local processing of stone and granite for exports The formal inauguration of the project would be performed by Pakistan Peoples Party Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari and Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah. Mr Memon said the average price of land in Marble City was being set at approximately Rs25 million per acre. Investors would not be required to pay the entire amount in a single instalment, as those unable to make a one-time payment would also be offered the facility to pay in installments. According to a press release, Mr Memon said that despite the country’s vast reserves of marble and granite, these resources had not been utilised to their full potential. He said agriculture also held fundamental importance in Pakistan’s economy, with a large segment of the population depending on the sector for employment. Pakistan needed to increase its agricultural exports and align agricultural production with modern industrial requirements. He said the Sindh government would welcome other provinces, including Punjab, adopting successful projects initiated by Sindh. Similarly, if the provincial government found any policy or project of Punjab to be more effective, it would be happy to adopt it. “We are all part of the same country and should encourage each other’s positive initiatives,” he added. He claimed that several industrialists who had established businesses in other cities of the country were now also interested in shifting their operations to Karachi and making fresh investments in the city. Special Assistant to the Chief Minister on Investment and Public-Private Partnership Qasim Naveed Qamar said the Marble City project covered an area of more than 300 acres along the Northern Bypass, with an estimated cost of $250 million. The project was being developed under a public-private partnership framework. He said the Sindh government was working on a proposal to provide electricity at Rs20 per unit for its projects, particularly in Dhabeji and Khairpur. He said efforts were also underway to provide industrialists in Marble City with facilities at the lowest possible cost, make machinery available on rent and provide access to the world’s most advanced equipment. Arrangements were also being made to offer electricity at rates lower than those charged by K-Electric, he added. Mr Qasim said the process of registration of investors and industrialists was being initiated, with registration scheduled to begin next month. Further facilities would also be extended to investors following registration. Published in Dawn, November 6th, 2026

Country’s external debt nearly doubles in a decade. • World Bank’s global debt report shows figure climbed from $68.7bn in 2015 to $135.1bn in 2025 • China remains Pakistan’s largest single creditor • Developing economies’ external debt rises to record high of $9.4tr ISLAMABAD: Pakistan’s total external debt almost doubled to $135.1 billion over the decade ending in 2025, according to the World Bank’s Inter­national Debt Report 2026 . The report noted that Pakistan’s external debt increased from $68.673bn in 2015 to $135.107bn in 2025. This included public and publicly guaranteed debt of $107.076bn, private non-guaranteed debt of $17.58bn and short-term debt of $10.45bn. Of the public and publicly guaranteed debt, $56.83bn was owed to multilateral creditors, $42.43bn to bilateral creditors and $7.8bn to private creditors. China was Pakistan’s largest individual creditor, with $22.4bn outstanding, followed by the World Bank with $19.2bn and the Asian Development Bank (ADB) with $16.83bn. The report put the average maturity of loans from official creditors at 16 years, with a four-year grace period and an average interest rate of 3.6 per cent. On the other hand, private credit carried an average interest rate of 8.6pc, with a three-year repayment period and a one-year grace period. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (Menap) region recorded improvements in debt-service and interest ratios. However, its external debt-to-gross national income (GNI) ratio rose from 26.7pc to 29.4pc in 2025, the largest single-year increase of any region, indicating continued debt accumulation. In 2025, China extended the maturities on $2bn in loans to Pakistan, while the International Monetary Fund (IMF) provided $2.3bn in new disbursements under the Extended Fund Facility and Resilience and Sustainability Facility arrangements to support the country’s long-term economic stability. Global debt at record high Overall, the borrowing by low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) surged in 2025, marking the sharpest increase in external debt in four years and a forceful return of private creditors to developing country markets. External debt climbed 5.5pc to a record $9.4 trillion as bond issues rebounded, the US dollar weakened and investors again showed greater willingness to lend. But the reopening of capital markets came at a steep price, especially for the poorest countries, which faced some of their highest borrowing costs in decades. Debt service payments also rose for a fifth consecutive year. Even so, stronger economic growth helped stabilise some debt ratios and net long-term debt transfers turned positive after years of outflows. The increase in external debt was even faster for countries eligible for International Development Association (IDA) financing, rising 8.1pc to $1.3tr, and for low-income countries, climbing 8.9pc to $262.4bn, the biggest increase since 2020. A weakening dollar amplified the rise in debt. The dramatic depreciation of the US dollar during the year accounted for 28.2pc of the increase in LMICs’ external public and publicly guaranteed debt. For several of the largest borrowers from concessional windows, currency valuation gains in 2025 not only offset principal payments made during the year but also, in some cases, partially reversed the stock reductions achieved through repayments in 2024, leaving reported balances higher at end-2025 despite continued debt servicing. Private lending, which is more susceptible to fluctuations in financial market conditions, pricing conditions, and perceived creditworthiness of borrowers, saw a strong rebound in 2025. LMIC debt stock owed to private creditors increased 5.2pc in 2025 to $5tr, a significant acceleration from the 0.6pc increase recorded in 2024. This increase was due to a combined increase in debt owed to bondholders and debt owed to commercial banks and other private creditors, which increased by 5.7pc (to $2.4tr) and 4.7pc (to $2.7tr), respectively. LMIC economies, measured by gross national income, grew by 5.1pc. This strong economic growth encouraged lenders to return to these countries, and many LMIC governments were willing to borrow despite relatively high interest rates. The countries that can least afford it are paying the most to borrow. Increased borrowing from private creditors hardened lending terms disproportionately for IDA-eligible countries, which faced an average interest rate of 8.2pc on new commitments during the year, the highest since the late 1980s. The difference in interest rates that this group of borrowers pays when borrowing from official creditors and rates on debt from private creditors widened significantly over the past decade, from 3.4 percentage points in 2016 to 5.5 percentage points in 2025. International Bank for Reconstruction and Development borrowers, by contrast, saw improvements in the terms on new commitments, with an improved 5.5pc average interest rate, down from 5.8pc the previous year. The report noted that the debt service burdens remain a pressure point for LMICs. Total debt service payments (interest plus principal) rose for the fifth year in a row, increasing 1.9pc to $1.4tr in 2025. Payments to private creditors drove the increase, with payments to bondholders rising 13.7pc to $363.1bn. Between 2022 and 2025, LMICs paid about $436.1bn more in debt service than they received in new financing. However, the trend reversed in 2025: long-term debt flows shifted from a net outflow of $118.4bn in 2024 to a net inflow of $45.4bn. Published in Dawn, November 6th, 2026

Shafay says standing by his younger brother. LAHORE: Punjab Commerce and Investment Minister Shafay Hussain of the PML-Q has said that he is standing by his younger brother Salik Hussain, Federal Minister for Overseas Pakistanis, come what may. In response to the ongoing controversy involving Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz and Salik Hussain, Mr Shafay said: “I have and will never distance myself from my younger brother. My brother is an independent person with his own independent views,” he told Dawn on Thursday. Maryam Nawaz has served a Rs5 billion defamation notice on Salik over his corruption allegations against her government, demanding that he retract his remarks. Salik, however, has maintained that he will respond to the notice. Defending his brother, Mr Shafay said he (Salik) might be privy to information (about corruption), which he was not aware of. “Salik Hussain never named Maryam Nawaz and never intended to say anything about her nor the Punjab government, but I believe he was referring to the systematic corruption that we all agree exists,” he said and added all politicians should be “more tolerant and should sit together to clear things.” He hoped that both sides should try to defuse and clear misunderstandings. On Wednesday, Information and Culture Minister Azma Bokhari said: “Shafay Hussain’s recent interviews have been supportive of Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, so we have no plan to denotify him from the Punjab cabinet. Shafay Hussain has rejected Salik’s allegations,” Ms Bokhari said responding to Dawn ’s queries. The latest exchange comes against the backdrop of a political split within the Chaudhry family following the ouster of Imran Khan’s government through a no-confidence vote in 2022. While Chaudhry Parvez Elahi and his son former federal minister Moonis Elahi aligned themselves with the PTI, Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain’s sons, Salik and Shafay, chose to side with the Sharifs. Published in Dawn, November 6th, 2026

UN Security Council adopts Pakistan-led statement urging diplomacy during wars. UNITED NATIONS: The UN Security Council on Thursday adopted a presidential statement initiated by Pakistan, calling on countries to continue diplomatic engagement even after the outbreak of armed conflicts and urging sustained efforts to secure ceasefires, prevent escalation and achieve lasting political settlements. The statement, titled “The Role of Diplomacy during Active Hostilities”, emphasises that diplomatic engagement remains essential during wars to protect civilians, contain violence, prevent conflicts from spreading and facilitate humanitarian assistance. It urges countries to use mediation, good offices and direct or indirect communication between warring parties to ease tensions and create opportunities for negotiations, even as military operations continue. The statement was adopted under the November presidency of Latvia’s Ambassador Sanita Pavļuta-Deslandes, who is presiding over the Security Council this month. Pakistan’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Syed Haider Shah, welcomed the adoption, describing it as an important contribution to international efforts to resolve conflicts peacefully. “The message of this Presidential Statement is both simple and powerful: Diplomacy must not end when hostilities begin. Indeed, it becomes even more indispensable,” he said during a press stakeout after the adoption. The Pakistani initiative builds on Security Council Resolution 2788, unanimously adopted during Pakistan’s presidency of the Council in July 2025, which reaffirmed the importance of a peaceful settlement of international disputes under the UN Charter. The latest statement extends that framework by focusing specifically on diplomatic engagement after armed confrontations have begun, a period when communication between opposing sides often breaks down and the risk of further escalation increases. The Council emphasised the importance of maintaining communication channels between parties to armed conflicts, both directly and through intermediaries. Such contacts can help prevent miscalculations, facilitate de-escalation and provide opportunities for political negotiations. “Through good offices, open channels of communication and continued dialogue, diplomacy can provide a vital bridge from confrontation to de-escalation and peaceful settlement,” Ambassador Shah said. The statement also identified several practical objectives for diplomatic engagement during active hostilities, including facilitating cessations of hostilities, ensuring safe and unhindered humanitarian access, protecting civilians and reducing the danger of conflicts widening into regional or international confrontations. It further emphasised that ending hostilities should not be an end in itself, stressing that diplomatic and political engagement must continue after a ceasefire to secure a lasting political settlement. The statement also recognised the contribution of individual UN member states that undertake diplomatic initiatives during armed conflicts. It encouraged them to continue using mediation, good offices and diplomatic engagement to reduce tensions and facilitate transitions from confrontation to peaceful resolution. Regional and subregional organisations are also identified as important contributors to conflict resolution. The Council welcomed efforts to strengthen their mediation capacities and encouraged closer cooperation between them and the United Nations. The statement further highlighted the role of the UN secretary-general in using his good offices, along with those of his representatives, special envoys and UN mediators, to promote dialogue and peaceful settlements. It encouraged the secretary-general to continue supporting diplomatic efforts before and during armed conflicts, including initiatives aimed at de-escalation and sustainable political solutions. The Council also reaffirmed that diplomatic efforts must remain consistent with the UN Charter, international law and relevant Security Council resolutions. It recognised the role of other UN organs in supporting peaceful dispute settlement, including the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in adjudicating disputes where states have consented to its jurisdiction. Ambassador Shah said the adoption brought together the Council’s experience in dealing with individual conflict situations under a common thematic framework, providing a political reference point for diplomatic initiatives in ongoing and future conflicts. “Today’s adoption represents a meaningful contribution to the Council’s thematic body of work,” he said. He added that the initiative reflected Pakistan’s commitment to multilateralism, dialogue and the peaceful settlement of disputes. The Council also requested the UN Secretary-General to continue promoting diplomacy, mediation and peaceful dispute resolution and keep it informed, as appropriate, of efforts in this regard.

PTI expresses concern over Imran's health, urges CJP to ensure court orders on treatment are implemented. ISLAMABAD: The PTI’s core committee has expressed concern over jailed party founder Imran Khan’s health, urging the chief justice of Pakistan to ensure the effective implementation of court orders regarding the ex-prime minister’s treatment. The party’s core committee met on Thursday and the gathering continued late into the night. It was held after reports that Imran’s blood pressure recently surged to 192 . A statement issued after the meeting said the committee had expressed “grave concern” over Imran’s health, citing the alleged lack of medical facilities and obstacles to his access to family members and personal physicians. The committee was briefed about Imran’s recent meeting with his lawyer, Salman Safdar, and termed reports about the surge in his blood pressure “extremely alarming”. “The core committee unanimously resolved that protecting Imran Khan’s health and life is an urgent humanitarian issue, and that any negligence, delay or irresponsibility in this regard is unacceptable. His health should be treated as a serious humanitarian and medical emergency rather than merely a political or legal dispute,” the statement read. It added that the committee demanded that the government provide Imran’s personal physicians with “immediate, unhindered and effective access” to him, make arrangements for all necessary medical examinations and diagnostic tests for Imran without delay, and transfer him to Shifa International Hospital for a complete medical evaluation and treatment. Noting that Imran had been in jail for over three years and concerns had been raised about his health, the committee resolved that any further delay in the fulfilment of its demand would be “unacceptable”. “The core committee appealed to the entire Pakistani nation, including overseas Pakistanis, to raise their voices immediately and forcefully to protect Imran Khan’s life and health. The meeting stressed that the gravity and urgency of this issue should be highlighted at the national and international levels,” the statement read. The committee appealed to the chief justice of Pakistan to ensure effective implementation of court orders regarding Imran’s treatment and give the matter “immediate attention” in view of its “exceptional humanitarian importance”. “The committee made it clear that implementing court orders is a constitutional and legal responsibility of the relevant government and administrative bodies, and that this responsibility cannot be evaded under any circumstances,” the statement said. It added that the core committee urged all PTI lawmakers, party organisations and office-bearers to raise the issue of Imran’s health, treatment and rights with “full force in Parliament, provincial sssemblies and other relevant forums”. The committee also expressed concern over an incident involving jailed PTI Vice Chairperson Shah Mahmood Qureshi in prison, “his fall and the resulting impact on his health”. It called for the relevant courts, the government and the prison administration to immediately transfer Qureshi to a hospital and ensure his complete medical examination and necessary treatment. Imran has been imprisoned since August 2023. His health has deteriorated over the course of his prison sentence, prompting outcry from members of the party. His eye ailment — right central retinal vein occlusion — came to light in late January, following which he has been taken to hospital multiple times. On Aug 18, the Supreme Court directed the government to shift the jailed ex-premier to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad, a day after the superintendent of the Adiala jail — where Imran is imprisoned — submitted a report to the SC on the ex-premier’s health condition. In the report, the jail administration said adequate healthcare facilities were being provided to the couple, with their health and well-being a priority. However, an annexure to the report stated that Dr Akhtar Ali Bandeshah of Pims examined him on Aug 1 and noted complaints of uncontrolled and fluctuating blood pressure, palpitations, headache and restlessness. The ex-premier had attributed his symptoms and stress partly to infrequent meetings with his wife, family and social contacts, as well as the absence of newspapers and TV. On Aug 10, the SC was informed, a medical board comprising Pims specialists also examined Imran after he complained of heaviness in the head and palpitations. It recommended a one-hour daily walk and relaxation in his prison routine, besides access to newspapers, magazines, television and books. The board also recommended more frequent interaction with immediate family members or his spouse, saying this could help control his anxiety and blood pressure. Subsequently, the court ordered his transfer to Shifa International Hospital. However, the government took the PTI founder to Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences, a government hospital, and subsequently transported him back to prison. At the time, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar had blamed “the security situation created by PTI workers on the way to and outside” the hospital for the diversion. The PTI has denied the allegations and accused the government of deliberately flouting the court’s orders.

Maliha Ali takes bronze at MMA worlds as Pakistan appeals semi-final decision. Maliha Ali fought with a fractured toe, a severely bruised eyelid and a partially dislocated jaw. She fought anyway. When Omar Ahmed, president of the Pakistan MMA Federation, asked if she could compete, her response was simple. “Sir, we fight from the heart,” she said. “These hands and feet are just not that important.” That courage carried her to the semi-final. It couldn’t carry her past the judges. Maliha’s run at the IMMAF World Championships in Tbilisi, Georgia, ended in a bronze medal and a dispute on Thursday, with the Pakistan MMA Federation filing a formal appeal over her split-decision loss to Russia’s Polina Baldina in the featherweight (65.8kg) semi-final. Baldina, 23, is a former world champion in a different MMA federation, having won a world title in Khanty-Mansiysk in 2024, and had won three bouts en route to the final. Maliha had a run of her own. She beat another Russian in the same division on Tuesday, two-time European champion Veronika Drozdova , by split decision, then reached the semi-final with a unanimous decision over Mexico’s Andrea Gabriela Guzman Salazar. When the final bell rang against Baldina, Maliha stood with her arms raised, believing she had done enough. The fight was close. No round was won clearly by either fighter. The second could have gone to Baldina. The first and third were tight, with Maliha landing the cleaner shots in the third. The scorecards told a different story. One judge scored the bout 30-27 for Baldina, giving Maliha no rounds. Another scored it 29-28 for Maliha. The third scored it 29-28 for Baldina. Three judges, three different scorecards, and the decision went to the Russian. “It was a clear win. We were literally robbed,” Omar told Dawn . The federation has submitted a formal letter to the Head of the IMMAF Refereeing and Judging Commission, requesting a round-by-round breakdown of the scoring, an explanation for the disparate scorecards, and a face-to-face technical review of both fights. Omar highlighted a deeper issue. In the letter, he noted that Pakistan lost a semi-final by split decision at last year’s championships as well. “When different explanations are provided for similar judging situations, it becomes difficult for national federations to establish a consistent understanding of the standards against which their athletes are being assessed,” the letter stated. Omar went further, alleging that ex-Soviet states favour each other in judging and dominate the refereeing space. He said Russia brought two fighters per weight class and a multi-million dollar budget through national sponsors, while Pakistan had zero officials on the panel. Wednesday had been a tough day for the family, too. Maliha’s twin sister Manesha, who won gold at the IMMAF World Cup in Angola earlier this year, also lost a narrow split decision to Poland’s Martyna Caruk in the lightweight (70.3kg) quarter-finals. The appeal is pending. Maliha leaves Tbilisi with a bronze medal and, her federation insists, a claim to something more. She fought from the heart. Now, her federation fights for her.

Turkish parliament approves Makkah defence pact with Pakistan, Saudi Arabia. The Turkish parliament on Thursday approved a bill ratifying the Makkah Agreement on Joint Defence with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, paving the way for the trilateral security pact to come into force. Lawmakers endorsed the measure by 279 votes to 119, with 398 of the chamber’s 592 members taking part in the ballot. The measure, formally titled the Bill on the Approval of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between the Republic of Turkiye, Pakistan and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, passed after a lengthy debate among parties. During the debate, ruling Justice and Development (AK) Party lawmaker Ziya Altunyaldiz stressed that the agreement aims to expand security cooperation in the region. He emphasised that it contains no approach against any third country and that its main goal is to prevent conflicts rather than escalate them. Opposition speakers raised reservations about the pact’s scope and oversight. Mehmet Guzelmansur of the Republican People’s Party said clear rules are needed so the agreement does not contradict Turkiye’s other international obligations. Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement at a trilateral summit in Makkah on Aug 7, pledging to strengthen collective security, deepen defence cooperation and promote peace and stability in the region and beyond. The pact provides a framework for collective assistance in the event of external armed aggression against any of the three countries, with the nature and extent of assistance to be determined collectively in light of the circumstances. Last month, the Foreign Office in Islamabad said Pakistan and Saudi Arabia had completed the ratification of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, as the three participating countries progressed on the implementation of the pact amid escalating tensions over attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Ansar Allah movement. “Pakistan and Kingdom of Saudi Arabia have already completed their ratification processes, while Turkiye is undertaking the requisite procedures in accordance with its domestic legal framework,” Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan had said at the ministry’s weekly media briefing. The pact moved towards implementation after an Oct 5 meeting of the alliance’s Strategic, Political and Defence Committee in Riyadh called for the immediate implementation of collective defence commitments and the rapid deployment in Saudi Arabia of military forces and capabilities already agreed upon, subject to the national legislation of the parties.

Saudi Arabia denies WSJ report claiming Houthis demanded $51bn to halt hostilities. Saudi Arabia has denied a report by the US-based Wall Street Journal ( WSJ ) that Yemen’s Houthis had demanded $51 billion from kingdom in return for a “negotiated halt” to the ongoing hostilities between the two sides. A report by the Journal claimed on Thursday that the kingdom had approached the Houthis “to see what it would take to arrive at a negotiated halt to the hostilities”, and the group demanded $51bn in return. The report, citing unnamed sources, further claimed that the Houthis would want to be “officially recognised … as the rulers of Yemen”. But Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Ambassador Rayed Krimly “categorically” denied the claims about “demands made by this militia”. “All of this is pure fabrication by the writers or their alleged sources,” he said in a post on X. The Saudi official further stated that “these militias turned against the Yemeni government, caused famine among the Yemeni people, and dragged Yemen into conflicts and agendas that do not serve Yemen and its people”. “They attacked commercial vessels in the Red Sea waterways, civilian and economic targets, and rejected all peace efforts. We also remind the writers that Yemen has a recognised government,” he said. The WSJ report and the Saudi denial has come amid renewed hostilities between Riyadh and the Houthis, linked to the larger Middle East conflict. The Middle East war erupted on February 28 when the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran, prompting Tehran to retaliate with strikes across the region. Then in July, the Houthis triggered a return to hostilities in Yemen when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace. The government retaliated by striking the airport, with ensuing exchanges unravelling a 2022 truce in Yemen’s long-running civil war. Since then, the Houthis have declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, attacking its tankers in the Red Sea, as well as the Saudi territory.

Asif sees attempt to set ground for 'alternative arrangement' in Punjab amid Maryam-Salik row. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif has claimed that Minister for Overseas Pakistanis Chaudhry Salik Hussain’s recent corruption allegations against the Punjab government are part of efforts to set the ground for an “alternative arrangement”. His remarks came during ARY News’ programme ‘ Khabar – Mohammad Malick Ke Saath! ’ on Thursday, when he was asked about his earlier statement, wherein he had suggested that Salik’s allegations could be “part of some future political agenda — to target Maryam Nawaz’s government and carve out space for himself in Punjab and at the Centre to secure his political future”. He alleged during the ARY News’ programme that Salik’s allegations “are part of setting the stage for some post-period”. “This statement was given selectively against Punjab. Corruption is prevalent everywhere in Pakistan. […] I have tweeted about it many times,” he added. Asif continued: “There is an attempt to create an alternative arrangement — to discredit incumbent people so that a fresh team can be presented. Whoever is behind this, that is what I was signalling to. Please do not ask me anything more than this; I can share my personal assessment.” He also alluded to “some wealthy people”, describing them as “carpetbaggers” who had been active in this regard for the past six to eight months in anticipation of a “political crisis”. Asked whether the “alternative arrangement” was specific to Punjab or was applicable nationwide, Asif said: “No, no. Some people are positioning themselves behind it; it is not something that is happening across the country.” “These people believe that the incumbent elsewhere may also become a party to the plan, but explaining it would be premature. […] This is my assessment for now; in the long run, the plan could be dropped as well.” Asif was also asked whether the “strong reaction” from the Punjab CM House to Salik’s allegations could be linked to Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi’s reported “close relationship” with the Chaudhry family, given that CM Maryam and Naqvi were “not known to have the best of relationships”. “Is this closeness a factor for concern?” the anchorperson asked. Asif said it could be a factor. “It is not impossible, […] they are pursuing their own interests. They believe that perhaps after two years, when the elections are held, […] they could become part of a new group” he said, adding that politicians of his generation had aged and were approaching retirement. Meanwhile, in a post on X, Salik said he had received a legal notice from CM Maryam and would file a reply soon. “Transparency is never meant to exist behind closed doors,” he wrote. The confirmation came after Salik, a day earlier, claimed not to have received the notice as he took a jibe at CM Maryam’s spokesperson in a post on X. What did Salik say? During a talk show on a private television channel on Monday, the Pakistan Muslim League-Quaid (PML-Q) leader praised former Punjab chief minister and his uncle Chaudhry Pervez Elahi , further criticising the incumbent provincial administration headed by Chief Minister Maryam and alleging that he regularly heard complaints of corruption. He also questioned lavish government spending , particularly the use of an official aircraft , arguing that public representatives should remain mindful of the country’s economic difficulties. He said officials using government aircraft should be required to demonstrate the tangible outcomes and public benefits of their trips. He also called for greater ministerial accountability, proposing that federal and provincial ministers should be empowered to perform their duties while also being held accountable for their performance. Salik’s remarks carry particular political significance given the fractured relationship between the Chaudhry family and the PTI leadership. Salik, the younger son of PML-Q president Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain, belongs to a family whose political loyalties have diverged sharply since the ouster of Imran Khan’s government in 2022 through a no-confidence vote. While Elahi and his son, former federal minister Moonis Elahi, aligned themselves with the PTI, the Shujaat family chose to stand with the Sharifs. Salik’s elder brother, Shafay Hussain, is also part of CM Maryam’s cabinet in Punjab. On Tuesday, CM Maryam said she had sent a Rs5 billion defamation notice to Salik, demanding that he retract his remarks. She claimed the PML-Q leader’s anger stemmed from neither corruption nor progress and the issue was that she had changed the deputy commissioner of Gujrat a few days earlier, whereas Salik wanted a DC of his choice to be appointed. Meanwhile, responding to Maryam’s remarks, Salik said he stood by his statement and had responded honestly to a question during the interview.

Indian Christians warn of attacks in West Bengal. Indian Christian leaders say they suffered systematic attacks on their faith after a spate of church vandalism and assaults in West Bengal state, they told AFP on Friday. Churches have been vandalised and pastors assaulted in the Hindu-majority state of 100 million people since Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu-nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) won state elections in May . Hundreds of Christians marched through the state capital Kolkata on Thursday. “For the last five months, we’ve seen systematic attacks being organised against Christians, and the pretext is unlawful conversions,” Herod Mullick of the Bangiya Christiya Pariseba (BCP), which organised the march, told AFP . Christian groups have been accused of trying to convert Hindus to Christianity. Christians account for less than one per cent of West Bengal’s population, according to the last national census. Mullick’s BCP said it had documented 48 instances of “vandalism and atrocities targeting prayer meetings, worship centres and churches” over the past five months, calling it “an unprecedented crisis”. AFP could not independently verify that figure, but other Christian organisations and research groups have also reported alleged attacks. The ruling BJP has rejected the allegations. A state minister has said freedom of worship must be protected, but that complaints of forced conversions would be investigated. The Catholic Association of the Archdiocese of Delhi said in a statement it was “deeply shaken by… the terror being inflicted upon innocent Christians in West Bengal”. The All India Catholic Union condemned a mob attack on a Bible conference in West Bengal’s Nadia district on October 9, when around 200 people stormed a church, smashing decorations and injuring at least six people. The Washington-based India Hate Lab research group said in a September report that it had documented 60 incidents targeting Christians in West Bengal after the BJP took power, including assaults, vandalism and raids on prayer meetings. Mullick said he was seeking a meeting with the chief of the Hindu nationalist RSS, or the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the ideological fountainhead of the BJP. The RSS and BJP have long accused Christians of forcibly converting Hindus, allegations the community vehemently denies. India has 1.4 billion people and more than two per cent are Christians, according to the last census. Christians say their religion has been present in India for nearly two millennia.

Eight killed, 30 injured in bus-truck collision on Hazara Motorway. ABBOTTABAD: At least eight people were killed and 30 others injured when a passenger bus collided with a dumper truck near the Havelian Interchange on the Hazara Motorway early Friday morning, rescue officials said. The bus was travelling from Gilgit to Rawalpindi when the accident occurred. Initial reports suggested that a tyre burst caused the driver to lose control of the vehicle before it collided with the truck, the Rescue 1122 statement said. Following the incident, Rescue 1122 Abbottabad dispatched seven ambulances and a rescue vehicle to the scene to carry out relief operations. The rescue operation, led by District Emergency Officer Hafeezur Rehman, was completed successfully. Rescue personnel provided first aid to the injured before shifting them to nearby hospitals for treatment. The bodies of the eight deceased, who reportedly belonged to Gilgit, were transported to different hospitals. One body was taken to Type-D Hospital in Havelian, while four were shifted to Ayub Medical Complex and three to the District Headquarters Hospital (DHQ) Abbottabad. All 30 injured passengers, including five children and six women, were shifted to Ayub Medical Complex for medical treatment. The condition of four injured passengers was reported to be critical, added the statement. A day earlier, a collision between a passenger bus and truck claimed the lives of 11 people and left 33 others injured near Pakpattan. Last week, at least five people were killed and 27 others injured when a passenger bus plunged into a drain in Punjab’s Hafizabad district.

Sperm whale spotted off Sindh's coast for first time: WWF-Pakistan. A sperm whale has been sighted off the Sindh coast for the first time, around 40 nautical miles southwest of Karachi, the World Wide Fund for Nature-Pakistan (WWF-Pakistan) said on Friday. The whale, estimated to be around 45 feet long, was encountered during an expedition by WWF-Pakistan board member Zahid Maker, the organisation said in a press release. Previous sightings of the species had been reported off the Balochistan coast in 2017, it added. Footage of the encounter showed the whale’s characteristic blowhole, distinctive skin markings and prominent hump. View this post on Instagram WWF-Pakistan Senior Director Rab Nawaz said the sighting highlighted the ecological importance of Pakistan’s offshore waters and the need to protect marine habitats and food chains that sustain large marine species. “Pakistan’s waters support an extraordinary diversity of marine life, much of which remains poorly understood and documented,” he said, calling for stronger conservation measures, responsible fishing practices and collective efforts to reduce pressure on marine ecosystems. Sperm whales primarily feed on cephalopods, including different species of squid and octopuses. In Pakistan’s coastal and offshore waters, their prey includes purpleback flying squid and diamondback squid. The mammals are deep divers, typically descending between 300 and 800 metres to forage, although they can reach depths of up to two kilometres. According to WWF-Pakistan, 26 cetacean species, including whales and dolphins, have been documented in the country’s waters. These include blue whales, Bryde’s whales and Arabian Sea humpback whales , as well as several species of toothed whales and dolphins. The organisation said its research and monitoring efforts had also helped document several toothed whale species in Pakistan’s waters for the first time. It stressed that sustained research, monitoring, sustainable fishing practices and stronger conservation measures were necessary to protect marine biodiversity in the Arabian Sea. WWF-Pakistan was established in 1970 to address environmental and conservation challenges affecting the country’s biodiversity and human population. The non-profit organisation works to protect wildlife, conserve natural resources and safeguard the environment.

Wave of bomb threats afflict European flights for third time this week. A wave of bomb threats were issued to passenger flights around Europe on Friday for the third time this week, as Spain’s foreign minister said the continent appeared to be facing “hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare”. Hoax threats disrupted dozens of passenger flights across Europe on Thursday, forcing unplanned landings by some planes and prompting fighter jets to escort or intercept others, a dramatic escalation after an initial wave on Tuesday. No explosive devices have been found and all planes have landed safely. Danish police said on Friday they were investigating threats directed at air traffic at Copenhagen airport, but that their immediate assessment was that there had been no danger to passengers. The airport said it was “operating normally”. Czech police said they had registered bomb threats to flights departing from and arriving in Prague. An airport spokesperson said they concerned four inbound and five outbound flights, but that no explosive devices had been found and no flights had been cancelled or diverted as a result. Shortly afterwards, an Italian airport authority source said a Wizz Air flight from Prague to Rome had been diverted to Venice and landed there safely. The French prime minister’s office said four new bomb threats had been made to aircraft flying over French territory, and that all had landed safely. A bomb alert on a Ryanair flight from Rome to Lisbon prompted a security operation when it landed, CNN Portugal reported. A fire truck is parked in front of the Vaclav Havel Airport in Prague as bomb threats forced airliners to make unplanned landings across Europe, in Prague, Czech Republic, on November 5, 2026. — Reuters Hallmarks of coordinated ‘hybrid’ attack Security experts said on Thursday that the threats had the hallmarks of a coordinated “hybrid attack”, although it was always possible that individuals were issuing copycat threats or acting on personal grievances. While no country has attributed blame for the threats, ⁠they come after a wave of sabotage attacks and attempts on targets across Europe ranging from German electricity substations to defence-related facilities in the Baltic region, supermarket refrigerators in France and elsewhere and Leipzig airport in Germany. Many officials have linked the campaign to Europe’s support for Ukraine in its war against Russian invasion , accusing Moscow of a campaign of “hybrid” disruptions that are essentially cheap to execute, easily deniable, and not expected to trigger an armed response. Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares told the national broadcaster TVE that, while it would take time to determine exactly what happened, “it cannot be mere coincidence that so many incidents with exactly the same modus operandi are happening across Europe”. “The most reasonable assumption is that we are facing an attempt at hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare,” he said, adding that Europe must be prepared for more such challenges. On Thursday, an airport source in Italy said bomb threats had been sent to several airlines and airport operators in Rome and Milan claiming to be from “fighters of the Male State”. Reuters could not independently confirm who had sent the email and there was no immediate indication of who was behind the other threats across Europe. Vladislav Pozdnyakov, a Russian blogger who set up an anti-feminist movement called the Male State in 2016 that was later banned in Russia, said the group no longer existed and was not involved in any way.

Nadra assistant director shot dead by unidentified gunmen in Peshawar's Hayatabad: police. PESHAWAR: An assistant director of the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra) was shot dead by unidentified gunmen near the authority’s office in Peshawar’s Hayatabad area on Friday morning, police said. The official was identified as Fahad Khan, the nephew of MNA Noor Alam Khan. According to city police spokesperson Alam Khan, he was shot in an area behind the Nadra office, within the jurisdiction of Hayatabad police station. Police reached the scene after being informed of the incident and recovered eight spent .30-bore pistol casings, spokesperson Khan said. The victim’s body was shifted to a hospital for a post-mortem examination, he added. The police spokesperson added that an investigation was under way to determine the circumstances surrounding the killing and identify the perpetrators. KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi termed the incident “absolutely condemnable and unacceptable”. He said he had directed the Peshawar capital city police officer to “ensure a swift and comprehensive investigation, with no room for delay, negligence or leniency”. “Every individual involved must face the full force of the law,” he said. Later in the day, Kundi told reporters that he had spoken with the Peshawar police chief and that the suspect would be identified using surveillance cameras and arrested soon. “There were land disputes ongoing; we are looking into whether that was behind the incident, or if it was some other issue,” he said. National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq expressed “deep sorrow and regret” over the official’s demise. He also extended condolences and sympathy to the victim’s family. “The (suspects) involved in the incident should be arrested as soon as possible and brought to justice,” the NA speaker said on X. KP has seen a rise in terrorist attacks over the past year. According to the Annual Security Report 2025 from the Centre for Research and Security Studies (CRSS), KP recorded a significant surge in violence last year as “fatalities rose from 1,620 in 2024 to 2,331 in 2025”.

Human bondage. BONDED labour is modern-day slavery. It exists in Pakistan as a system of generational exploitation sustained by abject poverty, debt, and feudal power. The recent praise for Pakistan from the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights for raising the minimum marriageable age to 18 is, no doubt, welcome. It follows the committee’s review of Pakistan’s second periodic report. But questions about the high numbers of child brides and bonded labour eclipse the compliment. Underage marriage is enslavement, while the purchase of bricks produced through debt bondage by construction companies and government groups continues to sustain the curse of bonded labour. Lifespans rarely outlast the loans driven up by interest charges. Generations inherit a cycle of debt and abuse. The scourge does not spare children, who begin life in inhuman working and living conditions. Entire families slog for pathetic sums far below the legal minimum wage. The Constitution outlaws all forced labour and slavery; the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1992, criminalises the practice. Yet, the failure to enforce the law and insufficient efforts to bridge the distance between constitutional rights and their fulfilment have forced poor people into a life of bondage. Punjab has over 210,000 documented kiln workers while more than 2,900 victims of forced labour were recorded last year. According to The State of Peasant Rights in Sindh, 2025, 1,311 labourers in the province were rescued from brick kilns and the farm sector. Patterns of enforcement are reactive and often set off by media attention or judicial intervention. Injustices — verbal abuse, beating, murder, and torture — prevail because spot inspections are absent. As per the National Commission for Human Rights, women routinely experience sexual abuse and forced marriages. Law enforcement and political quarters are notorious for protecting the perpetrators, instead of ensuring legal implementation. Systemic coercion will keep Pakistan from becoming a humane state. Published in Dawn, November 6th, 2026

Global tech stocks suffer bloodbath as US midterms fuel AI fears. Technology shares plunged on Friday after an unnerving rout on Wall Street as fears grew that Democrats would accelerate a backlash against AI after their crushing defeat of President Donald Trump’s Republicans in the US midterms . The Tokyo and Seoul stock markets closed out their weeks with losses of six per cent following the Nasdaq’s 5.5pc collapse on Thursday, its worst showing since April last year when Trump unveiled his wide-ranging global tariffs. “The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe,” said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club. “Big worries are colliding — the build-out of data centres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment,” she said. The London, Paris and Frankfurt stock markets shed around 2pc nearing the halfway stage despite featuring few technology firms. Elsewhere, the dollar firmed before key US jobs data on Friday, and oil prices steadied following steep declines this week. Futures contracts pointed to a rebound on the Nasdaq later this afternoon, but further declines for the broad-based S&P 500. Data centres have faced broad opposition from US voters across the political spectrum, and many midterm winners have pledged to put the brakes on such projects. Analysts said investors were also spooked by a call from progressive US Senator Bernie Sanders for a national moratorium on their building. The results compounded already heightened fears about the hundreds of billions firms had pumped into the sector and when they would see a return, while the recent spike in borrowing costs also fuelled concerns about their financial position. Bloomberg said the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had collapsed around 16pc this week, putting it on course for its worst run since April last year. On Seoul’s Kospi stocks index, chip giant SK hynix slumped 10pc and its rival Samsung lost 6.4pc. The Kospi more than doubled in value between the end of December and mid-June, when it hit a record, but is down almost 50pc over the past four and a half months. “The selloff shows that AI stock prices had been built on rosy illusions about the future, and now that illusion is gone,” said Dong Baozhen, chairman of asset manager Lingtong Shengtai. “The US stock market has been the standard-bearer and backbone of the global AI bull run. Now that backbone has snapped. Can AI bull markets elsewhere hold up on their own?” Tokyo dived 6pc on Friday as Japanese tech investor SoftBank gave back more than 10pc, while chipmaker Kioxia collapsed 8.7pc and semiconductor tester Advantest retreated 5pc. A 4.7pc drop for Taiwanese chip giant TSMC dragged down Taipei’s Taiex. “The blood is in the streets, folks,” wrote Neil Wilson, analyst at Saxo Markets, though he added that the sell-off looked “overdone”. “The fear is a total momentum unwind as Democrats pace the frontier and kibosh data centre build-out,” he said. Key figures at around 10:15am GMT London — FTSE 100: Down 2.2pc at 10,542.88 points Paris — CAC 40: Down 1.8pc at 8,057.43 Frankfurt — DAX: Down 2.3pc at 25,709.82 Tokyo — Nikkei 225: Down 6.0pc at 57,434.77 (close) Seoul — Kospi: Down 6.0pc at 5,059.69 (close) Hong Kong — Hang Seng Index: Down 1.3pc at 24,481.86 (close) Shanghai — Composite: Down 1.1pc at 3,649.18 (close) New York — Dow: Down 3.4pc at 51,523.06 (close) New York — Nasdaq: Down 5.5pc at 24,315.00 Brent North Sea crude: Down 0.1pc at $98.20 per barrel West Texas Intermediate: Up 0.1pc at $90.64 per barrel Euro/dollar: Down to $1.118 from $1.122 on Thursday Pound/dollar: Down to $1.340 from $1.345 Dollar/yen: Up at 158.24 yen from 157.83 yen Euro/pound: Up at 83.44 pence from 83.41 pence Sentiment shifts, cracks emerge Investor fear also centred on whether a stalling AI infrastructure expansion could hurt smaller firms whose capacity to raise funds has already been limited by higher interest rates and tighter financial conditions. Neocloud firm CoreWeave, which has become a barometer of investor anxiety over heavy AI spending and borrowing, slumped 10pc, while its five-year credit default swap spreads widened to a record level. “It’s pretty clear there’s been a real shift in sentiment,” said Michael McCarthy, chief executive for Australia and New Zealand at brokerage Moomoo. The selling indicates investors are starting to factor in increased local opposition to data centres, with analysts saying markets have yet to fully consider the cost such building has imposed on communities. Still, some analysts said the selloff was overdone and the bottom was not far off. “Today we are bound to see further liquidation of margin accounts, which suggests we are likely in the final stage of capitulation,” said Allen Huang, a vice president of Mega Financial Holding’s equities trading department. “Even TSMC hit its daily limit down circuit breaker at one point, which typically marks the tail end of a downturn. When TSMC gets sold off, that means all stocks have been thoroughly dumped,” Huang said.

Pakistan, UK agree to expand cooperation on counterterrorism, narcotics. ISLAMABAD: Pakistan and the United Kingdom on Friday agreed to enhance cooperation in the areas of counterterrorism, anti-narcotics, cybercrime and immigration, according to the interior ministry. The understanding was reached during delegation-level talks between Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi and visiting British Minister of State for Security Dan Jarvis at the Ministry of Interior. Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudry also attended the meeting. According to the interior ministry, the two sides decided to finalise at the earliest a memorandum of understanding on anti-narcotics cooperation, which would fully operationalise cooperation between the UK’s National Crime Agency (NCA) and the Anti-Narcotics Force (ANF). Naqvi told the British minister that Pakistan had foiled 330 cases involving narcotics smuggling to the UK over the past few years. The two sides also agreed to soon convene a meeting of the working group established between the interior ministries of the two countries. Jarvis appreciated the performance of the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) in curbing illegal immigration and acknowledged Pakistan’s sacrifices and efforts in the war against terrorism. He said cybercrime was an international challenge and all countries would have to work together to effectively address it. He added that Pakistan and the UK enjoyed excellent cooperation in various fields, which both sides wanted to further expand. Naqvi appreciated the progress made under the UK-Pakistan Serious Crime and Law Enforcement Project, a bilateral law enforcement and security initiative, saying it was proving extremely important in enhancing the capacity of Pakistani institutions. British High Commissioner Jane Marriott and relevant British officials attended the meeting. Jarvis is currently on his first visit to Pakistan to discuss regional stability, counter-terrorism, serious organised crime, illegal migration and visa fraud with senior Pakistani officials. He met with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and Naqvi on Thursday. Prior to that, Pakistan and the UK expressed concern at terrorism emanating from Afghanistan during their annual bilateral counter-terrorism dialogue in Islamabad.

PM seeks roadmap for ‘100pc’ digital payments system, stresses countrywide internet access. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Friday directed authorities to prepare a “clear roadmap and time-bound targets” for establishing a 100 per cent digital payments system in the country. The directives came during a high-level meeting he chaired in Islamabad regarding the promotion of a cashless economy in the country, according to a statement by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO). The premier directed the relevant officials to present a “clear roadmap and time-bound targets for establishing a 100pc digital payments system in the country”. “The issues faced by users in the digital payments system should be resolved immediately,” PM Shehbaz said. He further stressed, “To promote a cashless economy, the provision of internet across the country and easy access to technology for the public must be ensured.” “Promoting a cashless economy is one of the government’s top priorities, with its positive results already beginning to emerge,” PM Shehbaz was quoted as saying. He also commended the “ongoing successful efforts by the Ministry of Finance and all relevant state institutions” to promote a cashless economy. “The payment system through Raast QR codes is proving instrumental in achieving the government’s vision of a cashless economy,” the prime minister said, directing that the scheme to promote digital payments between consumers and merchants through Raast QR codes be continued under government patronage. The prime minister directed the launch of an effective media campaign to encourage electricity and gas consumers to make payments through QR codes printed on utility bills, and instructed all ministries and government institutions to ensure full implementation of the cashless economy plan. During the meeting, a briefing was given on the ongoing measures to promote a cashless economy, the PMO statement said. According to the briefing, work on the digitisation of payments in all federal and provincial government institutions was progressing rapidly, and payments in “most institutions” would be fully digitised by December 2026, the PMO said. It added that 100pc of the payments under the Benazir Income Support Programme were being made through digital wallets. “Work is underway to introduce a modern system for digital payments in areas without internet access,” the meeting was informed. “Efforts to establish infrastructure for internet provision across the country are progressing rapidly,” the PMO statement said. It added that cheque-based payments through Asaan Assignment Account will be discontinued from Nov 15, and instead will be made through the Raast digital system across the country. Drawing and disbursing officers have already been trained in this regard, it noted. The federal government has maintained that it is taking vigorous steps to stren­gthen the country’s financial system through fundamental reforms in the tax system, increasing the efficiency of the Federal Board of Revenue, promoting a cashless economy and using modern technology. The prime minister has repeatedly emphasised the need to implement digital transaction systems across the country, insisting that it was vital to bring transparency to the economy. In a bid to promote a cashless economy, PM Shehbaz formed a high-level committee in June last year. This July, he also directed that remittances from abroad be fully digitised as part of the drive.

Imaan, Hadi move IHC against conviction in security breach case. ISLAMABAD: Human rights lawyer Imaan Zainab Mazari-Hazir and her spouse Hadi Ali Chattha on Friday filed appeals in the Islamabad High Court (IHC) against their convictions by an anti-terrorism court in the security breach case. They also moved applications seeking the suspension of their sentences and release on bail pending appeal. The appeals were filed by advocates Faisal Siddiqui, Riasat Ali Azad and Zainab Janjua under Section 25 of the Anti-Terrorism Act read with Section 410 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) against the court’s order. On Oct 29, an ATC sentenced Imaan and Hadi to 10 years in prison each in the security breach case. The court also handed down one-year sentences and imposed fines of Rs50,000 each under Section 186 (obstructing a public servant in the discharge of public functions) of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC). They were also sentenced to two years each under Section 353 (assault or criminal force to deter a public servant from discharging his duty) of the PPC. In the identical appeals, the counsel contended that the trial court failed to meet the requirements of a fair trial and that the conviction was the result of patently illegal and arbitrary proceedings. It was argued that the charge was framed without providing copies under Section 265-C CrPC and that a plea of “not guilty” was recorded on the appellants’ behalf although none was taken. They further submitted that the prosecution evidence was recorded in the absence of the appellants and their counsel, contrary to Section 353 CrPC and Article 10-A of the Constitution. The appeal also challenged the jail trial, arguing that it was conducted in a manner akin to a secret trial and without lawful authority, and that the appellants were not allowed a proper and confidential consultation with their counsel. It further contended that state counsel was imposed on the appellants against their stated wishes and that the trial court proceeded with the case despite a transfer application pending before the high court, in violation of Section 526(8) of the CrPC. On the merits, the appeal argued that the conviction under Section 7 of the ATA was unsustainable because the prosecution failed to prove the design or purpose required under Section 6 of the ATA. It said the trial court itself described the incident as “a very common nature, ordinary type of incident” and that the evidence showed the appellants were on their way to court when they were held up at the barrier. The appellants have prayed that the impugned judgment be set aside and that they be acquitted. Meanwhile, in the accompanying suspension applications, their counsel sought suspension of the sentences and release on bail, contending that the conviction was rendered during the pendency of a transfer application and that the bar under Section 25(8) of the ATA was not absolute when read with Section 25(5) of the law. ‘Misuse of criminal justice system’ Separately, over 20 international human rights organisations, including Amnesty International, called on the government to “immediately and unconditionally” release Imaan and Hadi. In a joint statement on Friday, 23 organisations, including Alliance for Lawyers at Risk, Défense Sans Frontière, New York City Bar Association, Council of Bars and Law Societies of Europe, Geneva Bar Association, Lawyers for Lawyers, and PEN Norway, condemned the recent sentences and sought an end to the “extensive misuse” of the criminal justice system against the two lawyers. It said that the convictions raised serious concerns over anti-terrorism legislation being used “to criminally punish and intimidate lawyers undertaking permissible human rights work”. Referring to the case proceedings, the statement noted that the verdict was delivered despite a petition pending in the Supreme Court. “Proceedings in these circumstances raise concerns about respect for due process and the right to an effective judicial remedy,” the organisations said, expressing concern that the trial, which was conducted at the Adiala jail in Rawalpindi, did not meet fair trial standards. The organisations noted that the couple had been kept in a “cage-like” structure in the courtroom throughout the trial, rendering them unable to communicate with their counsel effectively. They also noted that the counsel was not given sufficient access to Imaan and Hadi. “The prosecution relied primarily on police testimony to establish the offence, while the defence were denied adequate opportunity to reasonably challenge prosecutorial evidence,” the statement read, adding that the couple had denied the charges and maintained they were being targeted for their professional work and activism. The organisations raised alarm that the “misuse of overbroad anti-terrorism legislation to the alleged removal of security barriers raises serious questions about the proportionality of the charges”. It observed that such legislation must not be applied “arbitrarily or disproportionately, nor used to intimidate individuals or punish permissible conduct or activities that do not meet the applicable threshold”. The organisations called for the convictions to be seen in the context of “successive, politically motivated, criminal proceedings” against the couple, which were “solely to punish them for and deter them from continuing their peaceful, permissible human rights work”.
