Police arrested at least 46 other people for allegedly criticizing the government. The Vietnamese government has failed to put in place legal reforms it pledged to undertake, Human Rights Watch said. In article 19.3 of the Trans-Pacific Partnership, Vietnam committed to “adopt and maintain in its statutes and regulations, and practices thereunder,” the rights in the International Labour Organization (ILO) Declaration, including the “freedom of association and the effective recognition of the right to collective bargaining.” Vietnam also pledged to ratify ILO Convention No. 87 on Freedom of Association and Protection of the Right to Organise by January 2024 but has yet to do so and continues to thwart the establishment of independent trade unions. Japan’s own Diplomatic Bluebook 2026 states that the Trans-Pacific Partnership “has great strategic significance in that it will establish a free and fair economic order with countries sharing fundamental values and principles, including freedom, democracy, fundamental human rights and the rule of law,” values that the Vietnamese government has systematically disregarded. Japan has not meaningfully responded to Vietnam’s worsening human rights record. In November 2023, the two countries upgraded their relationship to the highest level, a “comprehensive strategic partnership for Peace and Prosperity in Asia and the World.” “Japan should stop giving Vietnam a free pass on repression,” Doi said. “As one of Vietnam’s most important partners, Japan should make clear to To Lam that respecting basic rights and its labor commitments are crucial for a strong and lasting partnership.”

Thailand: Two Uyghurs at Risk of Return to China. Click to expand Image Detainees stand behind cell bars at the police immigration detention center in Bangkok, Thailand, January 21, 2019. © 2019 Sakchai Lalit/AP Photo (Bangkok) – Thai authorities should not forcibly return two Uyghur men to China, where they face grave risks of torture and other serious abuses, Human Rights Watch said today. The two men, whose names are not public for security reasons, were transferred from prison to immigration detention in Bangkok after receiving a royal pardon, apparently in preparation for deportation. “Previous Thai governments have kept Uyghurs in inhumane detention for years and then complied with Beijing’s demands to send them to China, where they were forcibly disappeared,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul should end forced returns to China and allow the two Uyghur men to travel to a safe third country.” The two Uyghur men have been detained by Thai authorities since 2014, when one of them was only 14 years old. They were serving a prison sentence for offenses related to an escape attempt from immigration detention in January 2020. On October 21, 2026, the authorities transferred them from Bangkok Central Prison to the Bangkok Immigration Detention Center Suan Phlu after they had served most of their seven-year sentence. Thai Foreign Ministry officials told a parliamentary committee that in August the Chinese embassy in Bangkok demanded their return to China. Under Thai immigration law and regulations, the two Uyghur men will be deported to China unless they object to the deportation and are resettled to a third country. Lawyers representing them told Human Rights Watch that they have already informed Thai authorities that the two do not consent to be sent to China. Thai immigration authorities have repeatedly refused to allow the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) access to the men to determine their refugee status. The Thai government is obligated to respect the international law principle of nonrefoulement, barring anyone’s forcible return to a place where they would face a genuine risk of persecution, torture or other ill-treatment, or a threat to their life or other comparable serious human rights violations. Refoulement is prohibited by the UN Convention Against Torture, to which Thailand is a party, as well as customary international law. Thailand’s Prevention and Suppression of Torture and Enforced Disappearance Act prohibits deportation when there is a substantial risk of torture or ill-treatment. In March 2014, Thai police in Songkhla province, near the Malaysia border, arrested about 220 Uyghur men, women, and children, charged them with immigration violations, and soon after transferred them to an immigration detention facility in Bangkok. In several separate incidents around the same period, the authorities arrested dozens of other Uyghurs and placed them in immigration detention facilities around the country. In July 2015, about 170 of the Uyghur women and children detained in Songkhla were released to Turkey. A week later, however, the Thai authorities forcibly transferred over 100 Uyghur men to Chinese authorities, who flew them to China. On February 27, 2025, Thai authorities took 40 Uyghur men from immigration detention and forcibly returned them to China. Upon the men’s return, the Thai authorities participated in a Chinese government-organized propaganda trip to show some of these men with their families. Despite promises by the Thai and Chinese authorities, there has been no credible monitoring of those Uyghurs since their return. UN human rights experts issued a statement on the one-year anniversary of the deportation and said the families of returnees “have received no communication, no confirmation of the place of detention or whereabouts, and no indication as to whether their loved ones are even alive.” Following the deportation, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said in February 2025 that it was “a clear violation of international human rights laws and standards,” and urged Thai authorities to “ensure there are no further deportations and the remaining members of the group, including potential refugees and asylum-seekers, being held in Thailand are fully protected in accordance with their obligations under international law.” Uyghurs are Turkic-speaking Muslims, most of whom live in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region in China’s northwest. Over the past 10 years, China’s repression of Uyghurs has increased significantly as the authorities have intensified a widespread and systematic campaign of human rights abuses against them, several amounting to crimes against humanity. The authorities have subjected the population to arbitrary detention, unjust imprisonment, mass surveillance, forced labor, cultural and religious persecution, and severe movement restrictions. Uyghurs considered to have left China illegally are, if forcibly returned, viewed with intense suspicion and subject to arbitrary detention, interrogation, torture, and other cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment. “Prior to the UN Human Rights Council’s review of Thailand’s human rights record on November 9, governments should press Thailand to immediately end its abusive treatment of Uyghurs,” Pearson said. “The Thai authorities should be protecting Uyghurs fleeing persecution, not jailing them, and certainly not returning them to harm’s way.”

Bangladesh: Academics Allegedly Targeted for Supporting Hasina. Click to expand Image The University of Dhaka in Bangladesh, July 1, 2021. © 2021 Sony Ramany/NurPhoto via AP Photo (London) – Scores of academics and students at public universities in Bangladesh have been arbitrarily punished because of their alleged affiliation with former ruler Sheikh Hasina and her Awami League party, Human Rights Watch said today. Any action to punish persons for their peaceful beliefs or without ensuring due process would violate the rights to freedom of expression and association protected under international human rights law and reproduce abusive attempts under previous administrations to control political opinion and expression at Bangladesh’s public universities. “Bangladesh has a long history of political debate in its universities, and only autocrats should fear such discourse, not a government formed following student protests,” said Meenakshi Ganguly, deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “Bangladesh needs to turn the page on the repression of the past, not repeat it whenever the ruling and opposition parties trade places.” The sanctions—dismissals, suspension, and teaching restrictions—focus on allegations that they were complicit in violence by Hasina’s Awami League government, which was toppled by student-led protests in 2024, allegations of other “subversive” activities in support of her party, or their alleged discrimination against students wearing Islamic clothing. Hundreds of students, allegedly Awami League members and supporters, are also being expelled, denying them their education rights. Human Rights Watch interviewed over a dozen affected teachers, examined university correspondence, and reviewed and analyzed a televised discussion and a video posted on social media. Interviews with teachers and students also confirmed expulsions, cancellation of exam certificates, or barring students from campus. According to media reports in August 2026, at least 404 more academics at 22 universities, who were part of a pro-Awami League Telegram messaging app group, have been put under investigation. “What is happening now is that the university authorities are targeting with false allegations the group of teachers who are aligned to the Awami League and did not support the 2024 student movement,” said a professor at a public university, who is not identified for security reasons. “We are not allowed to go take classes, we cannot do research work, we cannot do anything.” Hundreds of people were killed in a brutal police crackdown on the protests in July and August 2024, which forced Hasina to flee and paved the way for the return of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party to power following an election in February 2026. The activities of the Awami League were criminalized by an interim government in May 2025. For years, Bangladesh’s universities have been run in a partisan manner, employing and promoting academics close to the party in government and acting against supporters of other political parties. Starting in September 2024, the newly appointed authorities at Dhaka University, the country’s most prestigious university, ordered 44 academics to stop their work and restricted teaching assignments of another 25, without a transparent or credible disciplinary investigation. Subsequently, six of the academics were formally “temporarily suspended” following the findings of an inquiry committee, and similar investigations have now begun against another 14 teachers. At Bangladesh Agricultural University in Mymensingh, the authorities dismissed, suspended, or removed 12 academics and demoted or restricted the activities of another 34 after setting up an “investigation commission,” though this did not appear to comply with the university’s legally established disciplinary process. And in Sher-e-Bangla Agricultural University in Dhaka, 12 academics have been temporarily suspended and another 10 removed from academic activities following an inquiry process that teachers said they were not allowed to attend, an apparent breach of the law covering academic discipline. Another 85 teachers were denied promotions. In all, over 20 public universities have been affected, Human Rights Watch found. In March 2025, Dhaka University temporarily suspended 126 students, and withheld their exam certificates, after a fact-finding committee said it had found photographic, video, or social media evidence that they had attacked peaceful protesters. Cases filed with the police allege that another 277 Awami League students were involved. The university authorities have taken no formal action against them, but students and teachers confirmed that they stay away from campus for fear of arrest. Many of those named deny any role in the violence, yet the university has not provided a forum for them to answer the allegations. Among the academics affected is Professor Mashiur Rahman, from the Dhaka University sociology department, who since 2017 was deputed as a vice-chancellor at another university. He was told to stop all academic and administrative work on September 25, 2024. The allegations against him include claims that during the protests he “directly opposed the movement, calling it illegal, baseless and irrational,” during a July 2024 television discussion, although a video of the broadcast, reviewed by Human Rights Watch, shows no such comment. Another allegation is that at the prime minister’s house on August 3, 2024, he “incited genocide.” However, this was a meeting set up by the University Grants Commission that all vice-chancellors had to attend, and he has told Human Rights Watch that no evidence has been provided to him showing that he made such a statement, which he denies. On August 31, 2026, the university authorities recommended permanently suspending him, which he is appealing. The allegations against the sanctioned teachers at the Bangladesh Agriculture University center on their participation in a pro-Awami League march on August 4, 2024, the day before Hasina fled the country. A report by a Commission of Inquiry set up by the university refers to the march as a “terrorist” procession. A video posted on Facebook by the Bangladesh Agricultural University Journalists’ Association on August 4, 2024, and analyzed by Human Rights Watch, shows a scene from the march. In the video, a group can be seen walking on the campus chanting slogans. No direct confrontations are visible. Professor Purba Islam from the Department of Pharmacology was suspended on August 4, 2025, for her “sloganizing” at the procession, alleging “support for the oppression, persecution and genocide committed by the fascist and autocrat Sheikh Hasina.” No evidence of her shouting slogans is visible in the video. Professor Yahia Khandoker, from the university’s Department of Animal Breeding and Genetics, was also suspended on August 4, 2025, accused of maintaining “on the university campus, a clear position in favor of Sheikh Hasina’s mass killing.” Throughout the whole protest period, he said, he was with his family in Dhaka, not at the university. The High Court has stayed his suspension, though the Attorney General’s Office is appealing. Three academics, two of them in prison, were convicted by the country’s International Crimes Tribunal on crimes against humanity charges, with another awaiting trial. “Any acts of revenge against people who peacefully supported the previous government would show that freedoms of speech and assembly are not protected,” Ganguly said. “Universities should be places where people are free to express their views, not places where support is enforced for the government of the day.”

Burkina Faso: Islamist Armed Group Targets Civilians. Click to expand Image Ouahigouya, Burkina Faso, October 25, 2021. © 2021 Nicolas Maeterlinck/Belga Mag/AFP via Getty Images An Al-Qaeda-linked armed group killed at least 27 civilians in two attacks in Burkina Faso’s northern Yatenga province in September 2026.The group’s relentless, unlawful attacks put civilians across Burkina Faso at grave risk. The laws of war prohibit attacking civilians, and those who order, commit, or assist serious violations of the laws of war with criminal intent may be prosecuted for war crimes.Burkina Faso authorities should urgently strengthen protection for threatened communities, investigate abuses, and fairly prosecute those responsible. (Nairobi) – An Al-Qaeda-linked armed group killed at least 27 civilians in two attacks in Burkina Faso’s northern Yatenga province in September 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. These attacks violated international humanitarian law and are apparent war crimes. On September 1, the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, or JNIM) attacked a gold mining site in Soubo, Ouahigouya district, killing 24 civilians, injuring at least 20 others, and burning property. On September 5, three civilians on a motorcycle, including a child, were killed by an explosive weapon on a dirt track near Mera village, also in Ouahigouya district. Local residents believe JNIM forces had planted an improvised explosive device (IED). “The JNIM armed group’s relentless, unlawful attacks put civilians across Burkina Faso at grave risk,” said Ilaria Allegrozzi, senior Sahel researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities should urgently strengthen protection for threatened communities, investigate abuses, and fairly prosecute those responsible.” Click to expand Image Graphic © 2026 Human Rights Watch. In September and October, Human Rights Watch remotely interviewed 15 people, including 4 witnesses to the Soubo attack and 3 to the Mera attack, as well as human rights defenders and journalists. Human Rights Watch verified and geolocated four videos posted online showing the aftermath of the Soubo attack and analyzed satellite imagery and fire detection data to corroborate witness accounts. On September 1 at about 1 a.m., over 60 JNIM fighters riding motorbikes stormed an artisanal gold mining site about 1.5 kilometers northwest of Soubo village. They fired on civilians sleeping and working there, and at those trying to flee. “I’ve seen dozens of injured people, many by bullets, others because they fell while fleeing and fractured their legs or arms,” a 45-year-old man said. He said that those with gunshot wounds were treated at the regional university hospital in Ouahigouya. Witnesses said the attack lasted about two hours. Fearing further attacks, residents stayed away from the site for two to three days. During the attack, JNIM fighters destroyed hundreds of temporary structures such as sheds and huts, as well as motorcycles and mining tools. JNIM’s Sharia Committee, in a September 30 response (English, Arabic) to Human Rights Watch, acknowledged that JNIM forces attacked Soubo, but stated that the victims were members of the government-allied militias, known as Volunteers for the Defense of the Homeland (Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie, or VDP) and “not civilians.” However, witnesses told Human Rights Watch that soldiers and VDPs were neither present during the attack nor stationed at the site, although they occasionally patrolled the surrounding area. Mining sites are lucrative revenue sources for JNIM in Burkina Faso. The armed group leverages mining economies to generate revenue through “taxation” and extortion, recruit new fighters, secure essential supplies, and expand territorial control. Witnesses said that they believed JNIM, whose fighters include many ethnic Fulani, attacked the site in retaliation for the military’s targeting of Fulani people since 2022. Fulani communities, they said, had also worked at the gold mining site but had been killed and otherwise abused by the military and VDPs who viewed them as JNIM collaborators. A 45-year-old man said that while hiding in a pit to avoid getting shot, he heard a fighter say: “You chased us away, but you won’t exploit this place.” At about 9:30 a.m. on September 5, an explosive weapon detonated as people rode a motorcycle along a dirt track about three kilometers from Mera village on the route to Soubo and Sissamba. It killed the 40-year-old driver and his two passengers, a 65-year-old woman and a 5-year-old boy. Mera is near the Soubo mining site, in an area where JNIM fighters frequently carry out attacks. Witnesses said they saw no JNIM fighters nearby at the time of the explosion but had seen at least four fighters traveling along the track on two motorbikes the previous evening. A motorbike rider, 40, said, “I saw a motorcycle in front of me with three people on it, and suddenly there was an explosion…. Dust flew around like a whirlwind. I heard a loud bang that threw me off [the bike]. The explosion shook the ground.” Human Rights Watch could not independently verify the type of explosive weapon used or how it was detonated. However, JNIM has repeatedly carried out attacks in Burkina Faso using IEDs. A 2025 report by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines, a global coalition of nongovernmental organizations including Human Rights Watch dedicated to eradicating landmines and cluster munitions, noted JNIM’s use of IEDs in Burkina Faso. In 2024, Burkina Faso was among the countries with the highest rate of casualties—more than 200—due to landmines and explosive remnants of war globally. All parties to Burkina Faso’s armed conflict are bound by Common Article 3 to the 1949 Geneva Conventions and customary international humanitarian law. The laws of war prohibit attacking civilians, looting, and destroying civilian property. Individuals who order, commit, or assist serious violations of the laws of war with criminal intent may be prosecuted for war crimes. The Burkinabè government has an obligation to investigate and appropriately prosecute alleged war crimes committed within its territory. “JNIM forces should immediately cease unlawful attacks against civilians and appropriately punish responsible commanders,” Allegrozzi said. “Burkina Faso’s authorities should urgently improve demining efforts and increase assistance to victims of IED attacks.” Since the start of its insurgency in Burkina Faso in 2017, JNIM has repeatedly attacked civilians and forcibly displaced tens of thousands of people. Burkina Faso’s armed forces and VDPs have also committed serious abuses against civilians, especially Fulani, during operations against Islamist armed groups. In a report released in April 2026, Human Rights Watch documented that the Burkinabè and allied militia have targeted Fulani communities because of their alleged support for Islamist armed groups, resulting in the ethnic cleansing of entire communities. The nongovernmental group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data reported that JNIM carried out 125 attacks across Burkina Faso from January to August, resulting in the killing of 188 civilians, at least 16 of them in IED attacks. Explosive devices can be designed or fabricated to be detonated by a person’s presence, proximity, or contact. Such victim-activated devices function as antipersonnel mines and are prohibited internationally, regardless of whether assembled in a factory or improvised from locally available materials. They can also be made to detonate on command by various simple means or by a simple timer. Victim-activated IEDs are inherently indiscriminate weapons and are banned under the Mine Ban Treaty, which Burkina Faso ratified in 1998. Soubo, Yatenga Province, September 1 Witnesses said they identified the attackers by their clothes, including headscarves and a white flag with black writing, characteristic of JNIM. “They carried weapons and wore turbans,” said a 40-year-old artisanal miner and farmer. “They shouted Allah Akbar and shot at people at random.” JNIM is known to operate in the area and carry out attacks against government security forces and civilians. “The assailants began shooting everywhere and then went shed-by-shed,” a 37-year-old restaurant owner said. “I lay down in my restaurant and they found me.… They shot point-blank at two of my customers who fell in front of me.” She said that when JNIM fighters set her restaurant on fire, she had to get up to avoid being burned. One fighter wanted to kill her, but another told him to let her go because she was a woman. “They told me: ‘Tell your husbands not to come here anymore. These places belong to us.’” When residents who had fled the site of the attack returned, they found the victims’ bodies still on the ground or inside the mining pits. “I went back to the site three days later and saw the huge damage, a site covered in ashes,” said a 40-year-old artisanal miner. “I saw at least 20 bodies. The bodies were swollen and gave off a foul smell. I helped pick up the bodies and carry them for burial.” Residents said the bodies were buried in the cemeteries of the nearby villages of Soubo, Pirgo, and Sissamba. In June, Burkina Faso’s territorial administration minister had issued a decree suspending artisanal mining activities in Ouahigouya district from July 1 to September 30, to protect miners “from the high risk of landslides during the rainy season.” However, residents said, about a thousand people—mostly artisanal miners, but also shopkeepers, owners of small restaurants, and children—were at the site at the time of the attack. They said people had continued working despite the authorities’ suspension order, since officials never visited the site to enforce the suspension or check whether activities had ceased. “The terrorists burned a lot of property, huts under which there were small restaurants, motorcycles, small straw houses, mills, water pumps, and other equipment,” the 40-year-old artisanal miner said. “The fire spread from one hut to another. My barrel and my shed were also burned.” Human Rights Watch analyzed NASA satellite data and found evidence of numerous fires at the Soubo mining site on September 1 at 1:11 a.m. local time, corroborating witnesses’ accounts. Human Rights Watch also verified and geolocated four videos posted to TikTok on September 2 and 4, showing the destruction at the mining site. However, the videos only show a small part of the destruction visible in the satellite imagery. In imagery recorded on October 10, hundreds of structures are destroyed or no longer visible with burn scars on and around partially damaged structures, while others are completely destroyed. Satellite imagery recorded prior to the attack, on August 26, shows that the site contained at least 800 structures, consistent with witness accounts that at least 1,000 people were at the site. Click to expand Image Satellite imagery recorded on October 10, 2026 shows hundreds of structures destroyed or no longer visible at the Soubo gold mining site following the JNIM attack on September 1, 2026. Image © 2026 Planet Labs PBC. Analysis and Graphics © 2026 Human Rights Watch. Human Rights Watch reviewed a list provided by residents with the names of 24 victims, all civilians, including three women, ages 31, 36, and 37, and 21 men, ages 27 to 45. Mera, September 5, Yatenga province A farmer, 43, working in a field with other men near the road said he rushed to the scene after hearing the explosion. “When we arrived, we found a large hole at least one meter deep,” he said. “A few pieces of the woman's remains were not far from the hole – the woman had no body left. The man had been propelled far from the hole, near the bushes, as well as the child who had lost his lower limbs.” “The blast knocked the wind out of me, dust filled my throat, and I couldn’t see anything,” a 37-year-old man said. “The debris went very high before falling everywhere. I smelled a sharp, irritating odor, like sulfur.” He said that he and other people “took plastic tarps, collected the bodies and body parts, and carried out the burial the same day just after 2 p.m. in Yaoua village.” Witnesses said that after the explosion, soldiers arrived at the scene. The farmer said, “The military stepped in after the explosion to secure the area, searched for other IEDs and defused three of them, so we could safely take the bodies and bury them.”

COP31: Human Rights Critical for Climate Action. Click to expand Image A girl in her fishing boat off the coast of Malaita Province, Solomon Islands. © 2025 NowHere Media/Human Rights Watch (Istanbul) – Governments participating in the 31st annual United Nations climate change conference (COP31) should urgently act to protect the rights of communities displaced by the climate crisis and ensure that civil society groups can participate in the negotiations, Human Rights Watch said today. COP31 will take place in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20, 2026, under the shared presidency of Türkiye and Australia, on behalf of the Pacific Region. Negotiating countries and international climate funds should ensure that the needs of communities on the front lines of climate impacts and fencelines of fossil fuel extraction are driving the discussions, not corporate interests. “Intensifying climate impacts are already uprooting entire communities, yet those bearing these consequences are too often excluded from the decisions that determine their futures,” said Maria Laura Canineu, deputy environment director at Human Rights Watch. “Governments in Antalya should put affected communities at the center of climate action by ensuring that adaptation finance flows to displaced communities and to defending the space for civil society to hold government leaders accountable.” Human Rights Watch’s priorities for COP31 draw on its multi-year field research, including numerous interviews with displaced residents, Indigenous leaders, environmental defenders, and civil society activists. About 3.5 billion people already live in places and situations that are highly exposed to climate change impacts. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN body that assesses the scientific evidence on climate change, has warned that even with urgent government action to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, temperatures will continue to rise and climate impacts—from tropical storms to sea-level rise—are already making the places people call home unsafe, disproportionately affecting Indigenous peoples. At COP31, Human Rights Watch will present “Solwata,” a 25-minute mixed-reality documentary narrated and executive produced by actor and human rights advocate Mark Ruffalo, produced in partnership with the XR studio NowHere Media and Agog: The Immersive Media Institute. The immersive documentary is based on Human Rights Watch research on Walande, a community in the Solomon Islands, a Pacific island nation that was forced to plan relocation after king tides and rising seas eroded their small island home. The planned relocation of entire communities to safer land is already happening—including in Panama, Senegal, and the Philippines as well as Solomon Islands—and is projected to increase globally. However, few countries have national policies that protect relocating communities’ rights, and climate finance rarely flows directly to communities planning to relocate. Without adequate policies and direct access to funding, relocating communities frequently struggle with new human rights risks in relocation sites. At COP31, governments, multilateral development banks, and international climate funds should dramatically increase total funding for climate adaptation, including planned relocation, and ensure that Indigenous and frontline communities have direct access to funding to exercise their collective rights to self-determination. Financing mechanisms should include safeguards so that planned relocation is treated as a measure of last resort after all adaptation efforts are exhausted; that it requires free, prior, and informed consent; and that it guarantees access to adequate housing, livelihoods, food, education, health care, and cultural preservation. Rights-respecting climate action requires the full and meaningful participation of activists, journalists, human rights defenders, and Indigenous peoples’ representatives. However, Türkiye’s crackdown on freedom of expression, association, and peaceful assembly raises grave concerns about whether independent civil society will be able to participate safely at COP31. Turkish authorities have a longstanding record of suppressing free speech, swiftly and brutally dispersing peaceful protests, and jailing government critics, journalists, and environmental defenders. “The Turkish government has ignored the need for environmental protections and turned on local people who are speaking out against environmental damage to their communities,” said Deniz Bayram, assistant Europe and Central Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “States attending COP31 should speak out against Türkiye’s crackdown on environmental defenders and impress upon their hosts that civil society participation is critical to achieving COP goals.” Restrictions on civil society have repeatedly marred previous UN climate summits, including arbitrary registration hurdles, surveillance, and detentions. Meanwhile, despite scientific consensus from the Climate Change Panel that limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius prohibits new oil, gas, or coal projects, the Türkiye and Australia shared presidency has not called on countries to transition away from fossil fuels. At the same time, Türkiye continues plans for harmful coal power plant expansion despite court decisions which have rejected flawed environmental impact assessments greenlighting such projects. Australia has also continued coal expansion despite a high court finding that the state is responsible for emissions from burning exported coal. Burning coal produces dangerous air pollution that significantly harms public health, particularly for at-risk groups such as children, older adults, and people with chronic conditions, Human Rights Watch said. International human rights law, including the globally recognized right to a clean, healthy, and sustainable environment and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, obligates governments to cooperate internationally to mobilize climate finance and to prevent foreseeable human rights harm. Under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, to which both Australia and Türkiye are parties, and the European Convention on Human Rights, to which Türkiye is a party, the authorities are legally required to uphold the rights to freedom of expression, association, and peaceful assembly for all COP31 participants inside and outside the conference venue. “Communities on the front lines of climate impacts know best what they need to survive and adapt with dignity,” Canineu said. “The secretariat of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and attending governments should publicly press Turkish authorities to ensure respect for free expression in Antalya so that civil society groups and communities can be heard at COP31.”

US: New Congress Should Assert Oversight. Click to expand Image The US Capitol building in Washington, DC, November 4, 2026. © 2026 Umit Bektas/Reuters (Washington, DC) – The newly elected US Congress should prioritize respect and protection for human rights both within the United States and around the world, Human Rights Watch said today. Voters elected a majority of Democrats to control both the House and the Senate in the November 3, 2026 midterm elections. “This newly elected Congress will convene at a critical moment for human rights domestically and globally,” said Michael García Bochenek, interim US program director at Human Rights Watch. “Lawmakers should challenge the Trump administration’s many abuses, embrace the oversight authority provided to Congress, and act decisively to respect, protect, and fulfill human rights.” Lawmakers should address the widespread abuses in immigration enforcement by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and its agencies, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), which have resulted in arbitrary detention, serious injuries, and unlawful killings. The new Congress should reconstitute and strengthen transparency and oversight mechanisms, put in place meaningful protections against excessive force, and pursue accountability for officials and enforcement agents responsible for the many serious human rights violations of the last two years. The incoming chair of the House of Representatives oversight committee, Rep. Robert Garcia, has said that his focus will include “DHS and ICE abuses,” warning responsible officials to “lawyer up.” “The incoming Congress should prioritize rigorous oversight over the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Justice, and the Department of Defense,” Bochenek said. “Congress should restore gutted oversight bodies to full force. Without comprehensive oversight and accountability, abusive practices will most likely continue with impunity.” The new Congress should also mandate actions to repair and provide a remedy for harm and abuses committed by the Trump administration in its second term, Human Rights Watch said. These harms should include discrimination in voting, policing, education, and housing. To begin rebuilding the federal civil rights infrastructure necessary to tackle discrimination, which has been dismantled, Congress needs to conduct oversight hearings on the collapse of enforcement capacity at the Department of Justice, the Department of Education, the Department of Housing and Urban Development, and the Equal Opportunity Employment Commission. It should provide appropriations for these agencies that are explicitly directed to civil rights enforcement and pass legislation to allow private individuals to file suit under the Civil Rights Act to address disparate impact claims of harm that government actions have caused them. Congress has failed to implement adequate safeguards or oversight of the Trump administration, including as the administration has committed serious violations of the laws of war in Iran and continued unlawful lethal strikes on boats in the Pacific and Caribbean that have resulted in over 240 extrajudicial killings. Congress also oversaw the gutting of US foreign assistance and approved a bill allowing the government to claw back approximately $9 billion of previously approved aid, including critical support for human rights. The new Congress should look at opportunities to restore foreign assistance funding, particularly for human rights programs, in future appropriations processes. The new Congress should also demand that the Department of Defense release its report on an unlawful strike on a primary school in Minab in southern Iran that killed over 150 people, most of them children, and analyze whether dismantled civilian harm mitigation structures contributed to other unlawful strikes, Human Rights Watch said. The Trump administration has also removed tens of thousands of third-country nationals to other countries where they have faced human rights violations and a risk of onward return to countries where they are at risk of persecution. It sent Venezuelan nationals to El Salvador’s CECOT prison, where they were tortured systematically and subjected to other abuses, including sexual violence. The new Congress should reassert scrutiny over foreign policy and security cooperation, Human Rights Watch said. “Incoming members of Congress should strengthen the institution’s commitment to protect human rights for every person in the United States,” Bochenek said. “Congress should also embrace the guidance these protections offer for a rights-respecting foreign policy.”

UK Expands Human Rights Sanctions Regime. Click to expand Image Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband making a statement on Israel-Palestine in the House of Commons, London, United Kingdom, September 8, 2026. © 2026 Press Association via AP Photo The UK has significantly expanded its Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime, allowing the government, for the first time, to impose targeted sanctions on individuals and entities involved in war crimes. The new powers were approved by parliament yesterday. The previous framework, adopted in 2020, did not allow for such sanctions, providing, instead, for targeted sanctions only for certain serious human rights violations of the right to life, freedom from torture, and freedom from slavery and forced labor. Under the new rules, the government can also target those responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law, obstruction of humanitarian assistance, and violations of the right to liberty and security of person. This is an important step that means the UK can impose consequences for atrocities committed around the world. Although Foreign Secretary, Ed Miliband, announced the change in September while laying out measures to address Israel’s unlawful settlement expansion in the West Bank, the powers can also be used against those responsible for war crimes anywhere. Human Rights Watch has documented serious violations of international humanitarian law across the globe and called on governments to investigate individuals and entities with a view to imposing targeted sanctions. It is important that such sanctions are treated distinctly from criminal accountability. Sanctions should be used on those responsible for ongoing atrocities with the aim of bringing abuses to an end, and the UK should ensure that all persons affected by sanctions have due process rights to challenge them. Additionally, accountability for international criminal acts, past or present, should be implemented through criminal justice, including fair trials. In the West Bank, we documented the forced displacement of 32,000 Palestinians from three refugee camps in 2025, amounting to war crimes and crimes against humanity and called for targeted sanctions on officials including Defense Minister Israel Katz and Maj. Gen. Avi Bluth as well as criminal accountability. In Sudan, we found that the Abu Dhabi-based Global Security Services Group (GSSG), owned and run by Mohamed Hamdan al-Zaabi, apparently hired Colombian military contractors deployed to fight alongside the Rapid Support Forces, including in El Fasher, where the RSF committed mass atrocities. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, the M23 and Rwandan Forces forcibly recruited and detained thousands, including children, subjecting them to horrific abuse in “training” camps for which Rwanda Defense Force Special Force Commander Stanislas Gashugi and M23 commanders Léon Kanyamibwa and Bertin Masozera were responsible. The new powers give the UK the tools to act against all the above individuals and entities. To ensure the credibility of its expanded regime, the UK should use it in a principled and consistent manner, imposing targeted sanctions where appropriate to help end atrocities. It should also ensure its criminal justice system can investigate and prosecute those responsible for war crimes, wherever they occur and whoever commits them.

Hong Kong: Joshua Wong Gets Nearly 10 More Years in Prison. Click to expand Image Joshua Wong speaks to protesters near the Legislative Council in Hong Kong, June 17, 2019. © 2019 Kin Cheung/AP Photo (Tokyo) – The Hong Kong High Court on November 5, 2026, sentenced Joshua Wong, a well-known democracy activist, to 10 years in prison on baseless national security charges, Human Rights Watch said today. Two months of the sentence will run concurrently with his current national security sentence. Wong has been in custody since November 2020, when he was 24, and faces imprisonment until late 2036, when he will be 40. The Hong Kong government should immediately and unconditionally release Wong. Foreign governments should denounce the sentences against him and other wrongfully detained pro-democracy activists and impose targeted sanctions on officials responsible for Hong Kong’s growing repression. “The harsh sentence on baseless charges against Joshua Wong is cruel and unjust,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “Young people promoting social change are an asset for any vibrant society, but the Hong Kong government puts them behind bars.” To keep Hong Kong society subdued, and to reduce the chance of an international outcry, the Hong Kong government appears to have adopted the tactic of stacking charges against influential pro-democracy leaders to ensure their prolonged detention, Human Rights Watch said. Other notable Hong Kong figures who have faced similar tactics include Jimmy Lai, founder of Apple Daily, and veteran democracy activists Lee Cheuk-yan and Albert Ho. The court sentenced Wong, 30, under the National Security Law for “conspiring to collude with foreign forces.” The authorities accused him of “conspiring” with the activist Nathan Law and other “unknown” individuals between 2016 and November 2020 to urge foreign governments to sanction Hong Kong and Chinese government officials as they advocated for Hong Kong’s “democratic self-determination.” The prosecution relied heavily on the international lobbying and media advocacy that Wong and Demosisto, the political party Wong co-founded in 2016, carried out before the National Security Law took effect. Wong initiated online petitions, spoke to international media, and met with foreign officials to draw attention to human rights abuses in Hong Kong. He urged governments to sanction Chinese and Hong Kong officials responsible for abuses and to stop selling weapons to Hong Kong police that they use to carry out rights violations. Wong had mostly stopped these activities before the National Security Law became effective. Demosisto disbanded on June 30, 2020, and Wong resigned from the group. However, the government quoted social media posts by Wong as ostensible evidence that his alleged “conspiracy” with Law to commit “foreign collusion” continued after the law took effect. In these posts, Wong said he “would not change his views” and that he would “continue to seek support from the international community” in his personal capacity, while Law and others abroad would continue their international advocacy. The government also cited Wong’s subsequent opinion pieces and media interviews, though none directly called for sanctions, which the National Security Law specifically prohibits. It also cited his reposts of Law’s posts broadly calling for sanctions against Chinese officials and Hong Kong police. The court ruled that Wong’s offense was of a “grave nature.” The National Security Law sets prison terms of 3 to 10 years for “foreign collusion,” or 10 years to life for offenses deemed to be of a “grave nature.” Wong formally pleaded guilty on September 2. A guilty plea normally results in a one-third sentence reduction. But a sentence reduction cannot bring the term below the statutory minimum. Because of reporting restrictions on pretrial committal proceedings, when a magistrate determines whether to send a case to a higher court for trial, the public did not know the details of the accusations against Wong until the formal plea. The government enacted a law in 2024 to enable the court, on national security grounds, to deny the defendant’s right to ask the court to lift restrictions on reporting about the case. By restricting media reporting on the pretrial proceedings in national security cases, the government can control the narrative and undermine the fundamental legal principle of open justice. Since Beijing imposed the National Security Law on Hong Kong in June 2020, Hong Kong authorities have used the new legal regime—along with existing laws—to rapidly dismantle civil society and detain, imprison, or force into exile hundreds of activists and government critics. Wong has been in custody since November 2020, when he pleaded guilty to two charges of organizing and inciting an unauthorized assembly linked to the 2019 citywide protest movement. After that, he pleaded guilty to five more charges on separate occasions, including for violating an anti-mask law, participating in an unauthorized vigil for the 1989 Tiananmen Massacre, and breaching a court ban to disclose a police officer’s personal information. While serving these sentences, Wong was charged with two national security offenses, which carry far harsher penalties. In January 2021, Wong was charged with “conspiring to commit subversion” for participating in an unofficial democratic primary in 2020 and sentenced to another four years and eight months in prison. Before Wong could complete these sentences, the authorities brought the “foreign collusion” charge against him in June 2025, ensuring that he would remain in prison. Wong became one of Hong Kong’s best-known democracy activists as a teenager, after leading a massive 2012 protest against a government educational curriculum widely seen as political indoctrination. He became the global face of Hong Kong’s democracy movement during the 2014 Umbrella Movement and co-founded Demosisto with Law and others in 2016. The party disbanded on June 30, 2020, hours before the National Security Law came into effect. The National Security Law’s sweeping provisions have been used to punish peaceful protest and expression. Its use against Wong and others violates the right to freedom of expression under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which is incorporated into Hong Kong law through the city’s de facto constitution, the Basic Law, and the Bill of Rights Ordinance. “Beijing has paid no real price for its increasing repression in Hong Kong,” Pearson said. “Concerned governments should press for the release of Wong and other activists, impose targeted sanctions against implicated officials, and review their relationship with China more broadly in light of the deepening abuses.”

Bangladesh Labor Protests Turn Violent. Click to expand Image Garment workers demanding fair wage increases, payment of salaries, improved workplace facilities, and other benefits at a demonstration in Dhaka, Bangladesh, November 4, 2026. © 2026 Sipa via AP Images Bangladesh police have used batons and tear gas to disperse thousands of garment workers protesting for higher wages. Violence by thugs allegedly linked to factory owners and political parties, arson, factory vandalism, and attacks on police have all been reported. Consistent with international standards, Bangladesh authorities should ensure that police use force only when necessary and proportionate, and that those responsible for violence are held accountable. A garment worker, Toufiq Hossain, died on November 3. A co-worker who had been with him told Human Rights Watch: “We were returning to the factory [after lunch] when Toufiq got caught between protesting workers and men hired to tackle the protest by another garment factory. When I looked back, I saw Toufiq lying on the ground. The hired men had beaten him brutally.” The striking workers are seeking a monthly wage of 30,000 taka (US$241), up from the 12,500 taka set in 2023. The government formed a wage board on November 1, which announced that a new pay structure, once determined, will apply from December. “My rent is 6,000 taka ($48),” a 31-year-old sewing machine operator said. “Cooking gas now costs 2,300 ($18.50). I earn 13,500 ($108) [a month]. This year I can’t afford my children’s schooling. Tell me, what’s left for food?” Instead of addressing legitimate demands for living wages, Bangladeshi authorities are blaming the political opposition for instigating protests. On November 3, Dhaka police said they had arrested 33 supporters of the former ruling party, the Awami League, for sabotage. Others alleged that members of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) youth wing had marched against protesting workers. Three labor leaders were reportedly detained in Ashulia on November 3, accused of incitement. Police have also filed cases under Anti-Terrorism Act against thousands of unnamed people. “They took my husband away,” said a 28-year-old woman whose husband was arrested. “He had joined the protest for a short time. He wasn’t involved in any violence.” The BNP government promised inflation-linked wages before its election in February. An amendment to the Labour Act, adopted in April, provides for wage reviews every three years and prohibits employers from blacklisting trade union organizers. Bangladesh authorities should end the cycle of violence and impunity around wage negotiations. Global brands also have a role to play; they should always ensure that their contracts with suppliers don’t incentivize workplace abuses or make living wages impracticable.

Civil Society Call for Scrutiny of United States’ Rights Record. Click to expand Image Palais des Nations in Geneva, Switzerland, June 16, 2025. © 2025 Lian Yi/Xinhua via Getty Images The United States is scheduled to appear in Geneva on November 10 for its Universal Periodic Review, the United Nations’ peer review process of every member state’s rights record. But the US is unlikely to show: the Trump administration declared in 2025 that the US would not participate. After the US failed to turn up in November 2025, the review was rescheduled. Should the US again fail to appear next week, it should not be given another extension and should not be exempt from this process which, as the name suggests, applies to every UN member country. As part of the process, US and international rights groups, including Human Rights Watch, made 192 submissions highlighting a range of human rights issues. The civil society submissions paint a worrying picture, with a dramatic worsening of the US government’s rights record over the past year. At President Trump’s direction, the US government dismantled its civil rights enforcement apparatus. It has also violated the prohibition on non-refoulement and sent Venezuelan men to torture in El Salvador’s prisons. The Trump administration also continues to retaliate against opponents, restrict the rights of transgender people, and eliminate regulations that curb climate warming pollutants, among other things. In an unprecedented assault on the rule of law, the administration escalated its sanctions against the ICC, targeting the court as a whole. State legislation and targeted federal funding cuts have dramatically reduced access to safe abortion care and other reproductive health care in many states, curtailing women’s rights. During the immigration crackdown, authorities have separated breastfeeding and other parents from their children and have detained pregnant women despite a longstanding government policy that directs agencies to avoid this except in limited circumstances. The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights has highlighted concerns about deaths in immigration detention; harmful migration policies and enforcement; and sanctions against the ICC and Palestinian rights groups. The UN Special Procedures mandate holders have also raised concerns regarding: unlawful killings at sea; allegedly arbitrary removal of immigration judges and politicization of immigration courts; and unlawful use of lethal force by immigration enforcement agents. The US government is attempting to dodge international scrutiny of these serious and well-documented abuses. The Human Rights Council should not let that happen. This is a time for greater rights scrutiny in the US, not less.

A New Chapter for Corporate Accountability in the UK and the Road Ahead. Click to expand Image Smoke rises from a plant in Louisiana’s Cancer Alley, October 18, 2023. © 2023 Eli Reed for Human Rights Watch The government announced on November 4 that it will propose a law regulating the human rights impacts of companies in the United Kingdom’s global supply chain. The UK’s Corporate Justice Coalition, along with some businesses, have long led advocacy efforts for such legislation. The government’s announcement responds to some of those demands and marks a chance to turn corporate responsibility into meaningful legal obligations. According to the announcement, the largest businesses operating in the UK would be required to identify, assess, and address human rights abuses and labor exploitation in their operations and supply chains. Regulators would also be empowered to investigate goods suspected of being made with forced labor and, when companies have failed to meet their obligations, order their removal from the British market. If designed and implemented effectively, these measures could make a real difference to workers. But the opportunity extends beyond labor rights. Human rights and environmental harm are deeply interconnected. The UK should build on its announcement by extending mandatory due diligence to environmental and climate-related human rights risks. Human Rights Watch has documented how hazardous pollution, including from coal and oil operations, sickens nearby communities, and how logging and cattle ranching in some countries arbitrarily or unlawfully deprives rural communities of lands. Rising temperatures, extreme weather, water scarcity and pollution can threaten workers’ and communities’ health and safety. Workers in agriculture, construction, and other outdoor industries are often exposed to extreme heat as are garment workers sewing clothes in factories struggling with heat and increasingly unpredictable weather. The UK has an opportunity to develop coherent legislation that addresses human rights and environmental due diligence, bolstering responsible corporate governance and meaningful transparency. Done well, these reforms could help ensure that respect for people and the planet becomes part of how businesses operate, rather than another unfulfilled commitment on paper. For workers and communities whose lives are shaped by corporate decisions, this announcement is a reason for hope. The task now is to turn that promise into meaningful and coherent reform.

TERREMOTO IN TURCHIA E SIRIA:DECINE DI MIGLIAIA DI DISPERSI. Il bilancio sale a 11.200 vittime, si continua a scavare tra le macerie. Decine di migliaia i dispersi, tra loro anche l’italiano Angelo Zen. Sono ancora centinaia le scosse di assestamento tra macerie e devastazione: i soccorritori hanno a che fare con temperature rigidissime. Secondo l’Oms potrebbero essere state colpite 23 milioni di persone, tra cui 1,4 milioni di bambini. In Turchia, nel frattempo, monta la rabbia degli sfollati perché è stata descritta come una risposta lenta e inadeguata da parte delle autorità: sono migliaia le persone alla ricerca di un riparo. Erdogan ammette che ci sono stati inizialmente dei problemi. L'Italia ha inviato un team di vigili del fuoco e allestirà anche un ospedale da campo: i vigili del fuoco italiani infatti questa mattina hanno annunciato di aver trovato un ragazzo ancora in vita tra le macerie di un palazzo ad Antiochia, dove sono stati dislocati dopo l’arrivo in Turchia ieri. Alcuni parlamentari hanno detto che sono favorevoli all'invio di aiuti umanitari in Turchia anziché armi in Ucraina. Il sisma di magnitudo 7.9 dello scorso 6 febbraio 2023 è stato avvertito anche in Groenlandia, a oltre 5.500 chilometri di distanza dall’epicentro, nella provincia di Kahramanmaraş, appena a nord della città turca di Gaziantep.

CALABRIA: SALVIAMO LO SCOGLIO DEL DELFINO. Ad Africo(prov. di Reggio Calabria) e dintorni tutta la popolazione si sta mobilitando per salvare il famosissimo "Scoglio del Delfino" sita nelle mitiche scogliere di Africo. L'iniziativa è stata promossa dalle varie associazioni nazionali e internazionali affinché l'erosione calcarea e la stupidità d alcuni turisti non rovini questa meravigliosa forma d'arte scultorea che Madre Natura ci ha regalato. A causa di alcuni turisti col vizio di staccare, armati d martelletto, pezzi di roccia da portare a casa come souvenir, la parte anteriore dello Scoglio del Delfino è profondamente lesionata. E come se non bastasse, anche pescatori d frodo muniti di bombole e scalpello stanno minando le fondamenta a caccia di avalloni e datteri di mare. Per questo bisogna salvarla con un intervento di messa in sicurezza serio e risolutore.

WIJNALDUM COME PEDRO: DALLA ROMA ALLA LAZIO. TRATTATIVA IN FASE AVANZATA. Il trasferimento è a costo zero, la Roma non percerpirà nessun indenizzo da parte dei biancocelesti e risparmierà sull'ingaggio pesante del calciatore. Al PSG detentore del cartellino del calciatore andrà però un introito legato ai bonus di presenze o di raggiungimento di determinati obiettivi da parte del calciatore. Georgino Wijnaldum è in trattativa con la Lazio per un biennale da 3,5 milioni di euro e vestirà la maglia numero 30. ORIGI, MESSIAS, ADLI E 25 MILIONI PER MILINKOVIC-SAVIC. LOTITO NE CHIEDE 35!!!. Il Diavolo, dunque, ha intenzione di andare all'assalto del centrocampista serbo, classe 1995 , che gioca nella Capitale dal 2015 e che ora sembra arrivato al momento dei saluti. Nonostante il contratto di Milinkovic-Savic scadrà tra un anno, il 30 giugno 2024 , il Presidente della Lazio, Claudio Lotito , continua a valutarlo molto. Si parla di 35-40 milioni di euro, per un giocatore che, in fin dei conti, in questa stagione con le Aquile di Maurizio Sarri si è riconfermato come uno dei centrocampisti più forti e completi del panorama calcistico mondiale. Motivo per cui il Milan, pur di metterlo a disposizione di Stefano Pioli in questo calciomercato estivo, sarebbe pronto ad offrire alla Lazio 25 milioni più ben tre contropartite tecniche individuati in Junior Messias , Divock Origi e Yacine Adli. La palla passa a Lotito che attende un rialzo di offerta magari intorno ai 30 milioni e l'inserimento di tre contropartite tecniche di buon livello per concludere l'affare.

CONFERENCE LEAGUE :POSSIBILE 0-3 A TAVOLINO PER LA FIORENTINA. I TIFOSI VIOLA CI SPERANO!!!. Gli otto punti rimediati da Cristiano Biraghi in finale di Conference League contro il West Ham hanno fatto molto discutere, non soltanto per il gesto vergognoso. Tra le questioni affrontate anche quella dell’interruzione della partita e del 3-0 a tavolino, provvedimenti su cui l’arbitro Del Cerro Grande, da norma, non può nulla. È la Commissione Disciplinare Uefa a decidere. Andiamo quindi a spulciare il regolamento. Tra i casi in cui i club devono rispondere delle azioni della tifoseria c’è anche “il lancio di oggetti che possa mettere in pericolo l’integrità fisica di altri presenti alla partita o pregiudicarne lo svolgimento”. Il paradosso è che Biraghi, per sperare in un 3-0 a tavolino, avrebbe dovuto accentuare il dolore e farsi sostituire, invece è stato “colpevole” di essersi grintosamente rialzato. Per dare un’idea del modo in cui viene messo in pratica il regolamento, prendiamo in esame un caso simile: il famoso petardo in testa a Dida nel derby di Milano del 2004-2005. In quel caso le autorità capiscono che la situazione non può avere seguito e inoltre il brasiliano resta a terra. Per questo motivo, viene assegnato il 3-0 a tavolino ai rossoneri. In sostanza, il West Ham al momento rischia solo una pesante sanzione pecuniaria e la squalifica del campo nella prossima edizione dell’Europa League. Un caso simile, alla Fiorentina , è capitato nella stessa competizione contro il Sivasspor, in Turchia. Alessandro Bianco riceve un pugno in faccia da un invasore di campo della squadra di casa. Il calciatore rimedia la frattura del setto nasale. Per i turchi è arrivata una dura sanzione, più l’impossibilità di andare allo stadio per una giornata per i tifosi.

LAGIORNATA MONDIALE DELLE TARTARUGHE MARINE. Sono già una dozzina i nidi censiti dal network tartarughe marine del WWF in Sicilia (proprio in queste ore sono in corso le operazioni di verifica e messa in sicurezza degli ultimi), e uno in Calabria. Il Mediterraneo, sebbene rappresenti solo una piccola percentuale della superficie totale degli oceani, lo 0.82%, ospita una straordinaria varietà di vita marina. Con oltre 17.000 specie diverse, questa regione è un importante hotspot di biodiversità marina. E tra questa vasta varietà di specie, le tartarughe marine occupano un posto speciale. Nel Mediterraneo, tre specie di tartarughe marine hanno fatto di queste acque la loro casa: la tartaruga comune (Caretta caretta, l’unica che vi si riproduce), la tartaruga verde (Chelonia mydas) e la tartaruga liuto (Dermochelys coriacea). Le tartarughe marine trascorrono la maggior parte della loro vita in mare, ma, come altri rettili, respirano aria tramite i polmoni. La deposizione delle uova è l’unica fase vitale che avviene sulla terraferma, di solito tra maggio e agosto nel Mediterraneo. Dopo l’accoppiamento, le femmine raggiungono la spiaggia per deporre le uova, che vengono incubate dal calore del sole (e del suolo) per circa due mesi. La temperatura influisce anche sul sesso delle tartarughe neonate: temperature superiori a 29°C tendono a produrre femmine, mentre temperature inferiori generano maschi. Dopo la deposizione delle uova, le femmine ritornano alle loro zone di alimentazione, che possono trovarsi anche a migliaia di chilometri di distanza dalle zone di riproduzione. Una volta raggiunta la maturità sessuale, intorno ai 20-30 anni, le tartarughe ritornano alle stesse aree di riproduzione per deporre le uova. La loro capacità di orientarsi durante queste lunghe migrazioni è influenzata dall’incredibile abilità di percepire il campo geomagnetico terrestre, una sorta di sesto senso di queste antichissime specie. L’impatto dei cambiamenti climatici. L’aumento delle temperature globali influisce direttamente sull’habitat di queste creature e sulle risorse di cui dipendono per la loro sopravvivenza, oltre che sulle correnti. Uno degli effetti più evidenti è l’aumento della temperatura dell’acqua. Le tartarughe marine sono specie ectotermiche, il che significa che la loro temperatura corporea dipende dall’ambiente circostante. Con l’aumento delle temperature marine, le tartarughe possono trovarsi in situazioni di stress termico, poiché non sono in grado di regolare la propria temperatura interna. Questo può influire sul loro metabolismo, sulla loro capacità di digerire il cibo e sull’efficienza riproduttiva.

BONUS VACANZE: SCADENZA DELLE DOMANDE IL 30 GIUGNO. La procedura per la richiesta del Bonus vacanze va effettuata solamente online tramite la app “Io” da smartphone. Basta munirsi di Spid o della carta d’identità elettronica. Lo possono richiedere soltanto i nuclei familiari con un reddito Isee sotto i 40.000 euro e può essere speso solo per un soggiorno in Italia entro la fine dell’anno. Una volta ottenuto il Bonus, la prenotazione della vacanza non può essere effettuata su siti online: quindi non è possibile prenotare né con Booking né con Airbnb o con altri siti di prenotazione. Bisogna, invece, prenotare tramite agenzie viaggi o o tour operator tradizionali o direttamente con la struttura scelta nella meta di villeggiatura. Ecco gli step per fare la richiesta del Bonus vacanze: se non si è già scaricata la app “Io” in passato sul proprio smartphone è possibile farlo sia per telefoni Apple sia per Android; la prima volta che si scarica la app viene richiesta la registrazione che è possibile fare più facilmente digitando un Pin a scelta o, per chi è più pratico, attraverso il riconoscimento biometrico (impronta digitale o riconoscimento del volto); una volta entrati nella app, bisogna selezionare la sezione “pagamenti” e quindi il Bonus vacanze; a questo punto è necessario inserire le informazioni richieste, tra cui il valore dell’Isee; se tutte le informazioni inserite sono corrette, la app genera un codice associato al vostro Bonus vacanze con un QrCode; sia il codice sia il QrCode devono essere mostrati alla struttura al momento del pagamento. N.B. Prima di effettuare la richiesta del Bonus vacanze è bene tenere sotto mano sia la propria identità Spid sia la carta d’identità elettronica e i dati del proprio Isee (chi non lo ricorda può recuperarlo all’Inps o al proprio Caf). Il Bonus di un valore massimo di 500 euro è rivolto alle famiglie italiane composte da almeno tre persone. Per i nuclei familiari composti da due persone il Bonus vacanze scende a 300 euro, ma lo possono ottenere anche i single, in questo caso il valore è di 150 euro.

Una città d'argilla rimasta intatta per duemila anni: la meraviglia del II secolo a.C.. Costruita a partire dal II secolo avanti Cristo in un’oasi dello Xinjiang, Jiaohe non fu edificata con mattoni o pietre, ma scavata direttamente in un altopiano d’argilla. Considerata la più grande, antica e meglio conservata città di terra al mondo, fu uno snodo fondamentale della Via della Seta: il clima arido ne ha preservato per oltre duemila anni strade, templi e abitazioni. Carlo Nordio a Myrta Confidential: "Ho sdoganato il porno? Ho semplicemente messo dei paletti". In magistratura, a Venezia, Carlo Nordio si è occupato anche della censura di pellicole vietate ai minori. Il Ministro racconta a Myrta Merlino, su San Marino tv: “Era il 1982. Avevo appena finito l'inchiesta sulla colonna veneta delle Brigate Rosse. Avevamo fatto 150 arresti e il mio nome era stato trovato, ovviamente, nei covi. Ricevevo lettere con la stella a cinque punte, quelle cose lì. Il procuratore capo mi disse di stare tranquillo per un po' e di occuparmi di altro. Mi sono dedicato a reati economici e, tra l'altro, di reati contro il buoncostume. In particolare, a Venezia, un po' perché c'era la Mostra del Cinema e un po' per altre ragioni, si proiettavano questi primi film a luci rosse. Non è stata una sentenza, ma un'archiviazione. Ho posto dei paletti: se il titolo del film non è ambiguo, e in quel caso non lo era, uno sa che cosa va a vedere; se è maggiorenne; se c'è un rigoroso controllo all'ingresso, perché il film deve essere vietato ai minori; se i protagonisti sono tutti maggiorenni e non ci sono violenze. Se ci sono tutte queste condizioni, come fai a dire che viene offeso il senso del pudore di una persona che paga per andare a vedere quel film?”. Aggiunge però: “Quello che è molto grave oggi è che su Internet non c’è un controllo per i minori”.

L’iniziativa nasce dall’appello dell’Orchestre du Nouveau Monde, collettivo impegnato per la giustizia sociale e climatica, che dopo i lacrimogeni lanciati contro i suoi musicisti durante il corteo parigino del 17 ottobre ha invitato a creare orchestre di protesta in tutta la Francia. Hanno risposto 26 città, trasformando la giornata di sciopero nazionale in una mobilitazione anche musicale.
